|-
|'''Foreword'''

|-
|These lessons are an attempt to expand on the Google Wave Lessons, an excellent Lojban tutorial authored by kribacr, xalbo, and transcribed by Marenz, lessons which sadly only covered the first four chapters in this tutorial. It implements the newest rules of Lojban not covered by older materials such as What is Lojban? and Lojban for Beginners.&nbsp;<br><br>If you are new to Lojban, I recommend listening to any recordings you can find of spoken Lojban both before and while you are taking this tutorial, in order to make yourself familiar with the sounds and words of the language. Furthermore, try to say the things you read in Lojban accent if it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s reasonably practical. This can help your pronunciation a lot.

|-
|When taking this tutorial, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s best to pause between lessons in order to internalize what you have learnt. I have attempted to build these lessons from the bottom up and exclude any words or concepts that have not been explained in previous lessons. Once explained, they are used freely throughout the remainder of the tutorial. I urge readers not to pass any misunderstood content; if you have questions or are uncertain about something, feel free to ask the Lojban community, which can be found in #lojban on the Freenode IRC network. They will be happy to help.

|-
|In this tutorial, Lojban text is written in&nbsp;''italics''. Later, when used as Lojban loanwords in English sentences, they are not marked. Answers to exercises are displayed as a grey bar. Highlight the text in order to see it.

|-
|Lastly, I have as far as possible attempted to use the Lojban words for grammatical constructs:&nbsp;''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;instead of pro-sumti,&nbsp;''sumtcita''&nbsp;instead of modal and&nbsp;''jufra''&nbsp;instead of utterance. This is because I feel the English words are often either arbitrary, in which case they are just more words to learn, or misleading, in which case they are worse than useless. In either case, as long as the words are specific to those who are learning Lojban anyway, there is no reason for them to exist as separate English words.

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson zero (sounds)'''

|-
|While you are (hopefully) eager to get started on the inner workings of Lojban grammar, a short lesson on the sounds and writing conventions of the language is beneficial. Learning a language only by reading is hard, and it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s not easier if your internal voice is mispronunciating it.&nbsp;<br>For more details on vowels and consonants sounds used in Lojban, click on the letters described. They are pointing to Wikipedia articles which describe the sound and usually have an audio record of it.

|-
|'''Vowels'''&nbsp;<br>There are five proper vowels in Lojban and one semi-vowel. First the proper ones:

|-
|'''Consonants'''&nbsp;<br>There are seventeen consonants in Lojban and one semi-consonant. The Lojban consonants are the same as the English, except that Lojban doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t use the letters H, Q or W. Most of the consonants are pronounced like in English, but there are some exceptions:

Thus&nbsp;''ui''&nbsp;is normally pronounced "we", but&nbsp;''u<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;is "oohee". The capital version of this letter is&nbsp;''h'', the lowecase H.

|-
|Speaking of the letters, what is the name of them? You know, H is pronounced "age" in English, and K is pronounced "kay", rather different than the sound the letter makes on it own. How about Lojban? Well, consonants are straightforward: The name of a consonant letter is the sound that letter, plus&nbsp;''y''. So the consonant letters of Lojban, "b, c, d, f, g ...", are called&nbsp;''by cy dy fy gy''&nbsp;in Lojban. The semi-consonant <nowiki>’</nowiki> is called&nbsp;''y<nowiki>’</nowiki>y''&nbsp;(pronounced like an agreeing uh-huh).&nbsp;<br>Vowels&nbsp;'''would'''&nbsp;be called&nbsp;''.ay, .ey, .iy'', but that would be rather difficult to pronounce. Instead, they are handled by following the vowel sound with the word&nbsp;''bu'', a sound which signifies we<nowiki>’</nowiki>re speaking about a symbol. So the vowels of Lojban are:&nbsp;''.abu .ebu .ibu .obu .ubu and ybu.''&nbsp;<br>Lastly you should know that stress is placed on the second-to-last syllable in words with more than one syllable, and that one-syllable words are not stressed.

|-
|'''Correct pronunciation'''&nbsp;<br>You don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t have to be very precise about Lojban pronunciation, because the phonemes are distributed so that it is hard to mistake one sound for another. This means that rather than one <nowiki>’</nowiki>correct<nowiki>’</nowiki> pronunciation, there is a range of acceptable pronunciation—the general principle is that anything is OK so long as it doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t sound too much like something else. For example, Lojban&nbsp;''r''&nbsp;can be pronounced like the "R" in English, Scottish or French.&nbsp;<br>Two things to be careful of, though, are pronouncing Lojban&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''u''&nbsp;like Standard British English "hit" and "but" (Northern English "but" is fine!). This is because non-Lojban vowels, particularly these two, are used to separate consonants by people who find them hard to say. For example, if you have problems spitting out the&nbsp;''zd''&nbsp;in&nbsp;''zdani''&nbsp;(house), you can say zɪdani—where the "ɪ" is very short, but the final "i" has to be long.

|-
|'''Writing Lojban'''&nbsp;<br>As you have already seen, Lojban uses the Latin alphabet, though various Lojbanists have suggested different, usually self-designed ones. Furthermore, Lojban almost always uses lower-case letters. Capital letters are only used to mark stress in proper names, but people tend to avoid them even in names.&nbsp;<br>Apart from the letters, some punctuation is used:&nbsp;<br>A full stop (period) is a short pause. The rules of Lojban make it easier for one word to run into another when the second word begins with a vowel; so any word starting with a vowel conventionally has a full stop placed in front of it. Full stops are never used to end sentences.&nbsp;<br>Commas are rare in Lojban, but can be used to stop two vowels blurring together when you don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t want to use an apostrophe (which would put a H between them). No Lojban words have commas, but they<nowiki>’</nowiki>re sometimes used in writing non-Lojban names.

|-
|The following are found writing styles of different Lojbanists, but they are not conventional:

|-
|Spaces are usually used between words. They are mandatory between some words (more on that in lesson thirteen). Double or triple space is sometimes used before the beginning of new sentences. This is to clearly mark sentence shift visually. This might compensate for lack of capital letters which are used for the same purpose in English.

|-
|In òrder to visuàlly reprèsent the stress on the penultìmate syllàble, and bècause they find it visuàlly plèasing, some pèople use gràve àccents òver the consònant of those syllàbles.

|-
|Some people borrow other punctuation marks from English, even though they are not canon, and Lojban is equipped with actual words which should compensate for any punctuation one might want to use. Nonetheless, question marks, for example, clearly marks a sentece as a question and is much easier to catch with the eye than any word is, and so some Lojbanists use them. Quotation marks, parenthesis and exclamations marks can be used similarly. While this is not ungrammatical, since that doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t interfere with the sentences, some people think exotic punctuation creates an unwanted difference between written and spoken Lojban, generally a big no-no.

|-
|The following names are Lojbanized - their sounds are transcriped into Lojban and their ending sound have been changed to a consonant. The final consonant is necessary, because that<nowiki>’</nowiki>s how foreign names are differentiated from Lojban words. Again, more on that in lesson thirteen.

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons – lesson one (bridi, jufra, sumti and selbri)'''

|-
|A&nbsp;''bridi''&nbsp;is the most central unit of Lojban utterances. The concept is very close to what we call a proposition in English. A bridi is a claim that some objects stand in a relation to each other, or that an object has some property. This stands in contrast to&nbsp;''jufra'', which are merely Lojban utterances, which can be bridi or anything else being said. The difference between a bridi and a jufra is that a jufra does not necessarily state anything, while a bridi does. Thus, a bridi might be true or false, while not all jufra can be said to be such.&nbsp;<br>To have some examples (in English, to begin with), "Mozart was the greatest musician of all time" is a bridi, because it makes a claim with a truth value, and it involves an object, Mozart, and a property, being the greatest musician of all time. On the contrary, "Ow! My toe!" is not a bridi, since it does not involve a relation, and thus does not state anything. Both, though, are jufra.&nbsp;<br>Try to identify the bridi among these English jufra:

|-
|1. "I hate it when you do that."

|-
|2. "Runs."

|-
|3. "Woah, that looks delicious!"

|-
|4. "Geez, not again."

|-
|5. "No, I own three cars"

|-
|6. "Nineteen minutes past eight."

|-
|7. "This Saturday, yes."

|-
|&nbsp;&nbsp;<br>Answer:&nbsp;1, 3 and 5 are bridi. 2 contains no objects and the rest contain no relation or claim of a property.

|-
|Put in Lojban terms, a bridi consists of one&nbsp;''selbri'', and one or more&nbsp;''sumti''. The selbri is the relation or claim about the object, and the sumti are the objects which are in a relation. Note that "object" is not a perfect translation of "sumti", since "sumti" can refer to not just physical objects, but can also purely abstract things like "The idea of warfare". A better translation would be something like "subject, direct or indirect object" for sumti, and "verb" for selbri, though, as we will see, this is not optimal either.&nbsp;<br>We can now write the first important lesson down:&nbsp;<br>bridi = selbri <nowiki>+</nowiki> one or more sumti&nbsp;<br>Put another way, a bridi states that some sumti do/are something explained by a selbri.

|-
|Identify the sumti and selbri equivalents in these English jufra:&nbsp;<br>"I will pick up my daughters with my car"

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;selbri: "pick up (with)". sumti: "I", "my daughters", "my car"

|-
|"He bought 5 new shirts from Mark for just two hundred euro!"

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;selbri: "bought (from) (for)" sumti: "He", "5 new shirts", "Mark" and "two hundred euros"

|-
|Since these concepts are so fundamental to Lojban, let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s have a third example: "So far, the EPA has done nothing about the amount of sulphur dioxide."

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;selbri: "has done (about)" sumti: "The EPA", "nothing" and "the amount of sulphur dioxide"

|-
|Now try begin making Lojban bridi. For this you will need to use some words, which can act as selbri:&nbsp;<br>'''''dunda'''''&nbsp;x1 gives x2 to x3 (without payment)&nbsp;<br>'''''pelxu'''''&nbsp;x1 is yellow&nbsp;<br>'''''zdani'''''&nbsp;x1 is a home of x2

|-
|Notice that these words meaning "give", "yellow" and "home" would be considered a verb, an adjective and a noun in English. In Lojban, there are no such categories and no such distinction.&nbsp;''dunda''&nbsp;can be translated "gives" (verb), "is a giver" (noun), "is giving" (adjective) as well as to an adverb form. They all act as selbri, and are used in the same way.

|-
|As well as a few words, which can act as sumti:&nbsp;<br>'''''mi'''''&nbsp;"I" or "we" – the one or those who are speaking.&nbsp;<br>'''''ti'''''&nbsp;"this" – a close thing or event nearby which can be pointed to by the speaker.&nbsp;<br>'''''do'''''&nbsp;"you" – the one or those who are being spoken to.

|-
|See the strange translations of the selbri above - especially the x1, x2 and x3? Those are called sumti places. They are places where sumti can go to fill a bridi. Filling a sumti in a place states that the sumti fits in that place. The second place of&nbsp;''dunda'', for example, x2, is the thing being given. The third is the object which receives the thing. Notice also that the translation of&nbsp;''dunda''&nbsp;has the word "to" in it. This is because, while this word is needed in English to signify the receiver, the receiver is in the third sumti place of&nbsp;''dunda''. So when you fill the third sumti place of&nbsp;''dunda'', the sumti you fill in is always the receiver, and you don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t need an equivalent to the word "to"!

|-
|To say a bridi, you simply say the x1 sumti first, then the selbri, then any other sumti.&nbsp;<br>Usual bridi: <nowiki>{</nowiki>x1 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;'''<nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki>'''&nbsp;<nowiki>{</nowiki>x2 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>x3 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>x4 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>x5 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>and so on<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>The order can be played around with, but for now, we stick with the usual form. To say "I give this to you" you just say&nbsp;''mi dunda ti do'', with the three sumti at the right places.

|-
|So, how would you say "This is a home of me"?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''ti zdani mi''

|-
|Try a few more in order to get the idea of a place structure sink in.

|-
|"You give this to me"?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''do dunda ti mi''

|-
|And translate&nbsp;''ti pelxu''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"This is yellow."

|-
|Quite easy once you get the hang of it, right?

|-
|Multiple bridi after each other are separated by&nbsp;''.i''&nbsp;This is the Lojban equivalent of full stop, but it usually goes before bridi instead of after them. It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s often left out before the first bridi, though, as in all these examples:&nbsp;<br>'''''.i'''''&nbsp;Sentence separator. Separates any two jufra (and therefore also bridi).

|-
|''ti zdani mi .i ti pelxu''&nbsp;"This is a home to me. This is yellow."

|-
|Before you move on to the next lesson, I recommend that you take a break for at least seven minutes to let the information sink in.

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons – lesson two (FA and zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e)'''

|-
|Most selbri have from one to five sumti places, but some have more. Here is a selbri with four sumti places:&nbsp;<br>'''''vecnu'''''&nbsp;x1 sells x2 to x3 for price x4

|-
|If I want to say "I sell this", it would be too much to have to fill the sumti places x3 and x4, which specify who I sell the thing to, and for what price. Luckily, I don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t need to. sumti places can be filled with&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''.&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;indicates to us that the value of the sumti place is unspecified because it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s unimportant or can be determined from context.&nbsp;<br>'''''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;"something" Fills a sumti place with something, but does not state what.

|-
|So to say "I sell to you", I could say&nbsp;''mi vecnu zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e do zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;– I sell something to you for some price.&nbsp;<br>How would you say: "That<nowiki>’</nowiki>s a home (for somebody)"?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''ti zdani zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''

|-
|How about "(someone) gives this to (someone)"?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e dunda ti zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''

|-
|Still, filling out three zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e just to say that a thing is being sold takes time. Therefore you don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t need to write all the&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;in a bridi. The rule simply is that if you leave out any sumti, they will be considered as if they contained&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''. If the bridi begins with a selbri, the x1 is presumed to be omitted and it becomes&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''.&nbsp;<br>Try it out. What<nowiki>’</nowiki>s Lojban for "I sell"?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi vecnu''

|-
|And what does&nbsp;''zdani mi''&nbsp;mean?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"Something is a home of me" or just "I have a home."

|-
|As mentioned earlier, the form doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t have to be <nowiki>{</nowiki>x1 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>x2 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>x3 sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> (ect.) In fact, you can place the selbri anywhere you want, just not at the beginning of the bridi. If you do that, the x1 is considered left out and filled with&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;instead. So the following three jufra are all the exactly same bridi:&nbsp;<br>''mi dunda ti do''&nbsp;<br>''mi ti dunda do''&nbsp;<br>''mi ti do dunda''

|-
|Sometimes this is used for poetic effect. "You sell yourself" could be&nbsp;''do do vecnu'', which sounds better than&nbsp;''do vecnu do''. Or it can be used for clarity if the selbri is very long and therefore better be left at the end of the bridi.

|-
|There are also several ways to play around with the order of the sumti inside the bridi. The easiest one is by using the words&nbsp;''fa'',&nbsp;''fe'',&nbsp;''fi'',&nbsp;''fo''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''fu''. Notice that the vowels are the five vowels in the Lojban alphabet in order. Using one of these words marks that the next sumti will fill the x1, x2, x3, x4 and x5 respectively. The next sumti after that will be presumed to fill a slot one greater than the previous. To use an example:&nbsp;<br>''dunda fa do fe ti do''&nbsp;– "Giving by you of this thing to you".&nbsp;''fa''&nbsp;marks the x1, the giver, which is you.&nbsp;''fe''&nbsp;marks the thing being given, the x2. Sumti counting then continues from&nbsp;''fe'', meaning that the last sumti fills x3, the object receiving.

|-
|Attempt to translate the following three sentences:

|-
|''mi vecnu fo ti fe do''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"I sell, for the price of this, you". or "I sell you for the price of this" (probably pointing to a bunch of money)

|-
|''zdani fe ti''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"This has a home". Here, the fe is redundant.

|-
|''vecnu zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e mi ti fa do''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"You sell something to me for this price"

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons – lesson three (tanru and lo)'''

|-
|In this lesson, you will become familiar with the concept of a&nbsp;''tanru''. A tanru is formed when a selbri is put in front of another selbri, modifying its meaning. A tanru is itself a selbri, and can combine with other selbri or tanru to form more complex tanru. Thus&nbsp;''zdani vecnu''&nbsp;is a tanru, as well as&nbsp;''pelxu zdani vecnu'', which is made from the tanru&nbsp;''pelxu zdani''&nbsp;and the single brivla word&nbsp;''vecnu''. To understand the concept of tanru, consider the English noun combination "lemon tree". If you didn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t know what a lemon tree was, but had heard about both lemons and trees, you would not be able to deduce what a lemon tree was. Perhaps a lemon-colored tree, or a tree shaped like a lemon, or a tree whose bark tastes like lemon. The only things you could know for sure would be that it would be a tree, and it would be lemon-like in some way.&nbsp;<br>A tanru is closely analogous to this. It cannot be said exactly what a&nbsp;''zdani vecnu''&nbsp;is, but it can be said that it is definitely a vecnu, and that it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s zdani-like in some way. And it could be zdani-like in any way. In theory, no matter how silly or absurd the connection to zdani was, it could still truly be a&nbsp;''zdani vecnu''. However, it must actually be a vecnu in the ordinary sense in order for the tanru to apply. You could gloss&nbsp;''zdani vecnu''&nbsp;as "home seller", or even better but worse sounding "a home-type-of seller". The place structure of a tanru is always that of the rightmost selbri. It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s also said that the left selbri modifies the right selbri.&nbsp;<br>"Really?", you ask, sceptically, "It doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t matter how silly the connection to the left word in a tanru is, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s still true? So I could call all sellers for&nbsp;''zdani vecnu''&nbsp;and then make up some silly excuse why I think it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s zdani-like?"&nbsp;<br>Well yes, but then you<nowiki>’</nowiki>d be a dick. Or at least you<nowiki>’</nowiki>d be intentionally misleading. In general, you should use a tanru when it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s obvious how the left word relates to the right.

|-
|Attempt to translate the following:&nbsp;''ti pelxu zdani do''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"That is a yellow home for you" Again, we don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t know in which way it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s yellow. Probably it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s painted yellow, but we don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t know for sure.

|-
|''mi vecnu dunda''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"I sell-like give". What can that mean? No idea. It certainly doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t mean that you sold something, since, by definition of&nbsp;''dunda'', there can be no payment involved. It has to be a giveaway, but be sell-like in some aspect.

|-
|And now for something completely different. What if I wanted to say I sold to a German?&nbsp;<br>'''''dotco'''''&nbsp;x1 is German/reflects German culture in aspect x2

|-
|I can<nowiki>’</nowiki>t say&nbsp;''mi vecnu zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e dotco''&nbsp;because that would leave two selbri in a bridi, which is not permitted. I could say&nbsp;''mi dotco vecnu''&nbsp;but that would be unnecessary vague - I could sell in a German way. Likewise, if I want to say "I am friends with an American", what should I say?&nbsp;<br>'''''pendo'''''&nbsp;1x is a friend of x2&nbsp;<br>'''''merko'''''&nbsp;x1 is American/reflect US culture in aspect x2

|-
|Again, the obvious would be to say&nbsp;''mi pendo merko'', but that would form a tanru, meaning "I am friend-like American", which is wrong. What we really want to is to take the selbri&nbsp;''merko''&nbsp;and transform it into a sumti so it can be used in the selbri&nbsp;''pendo''. This is done by the two words&nbsp;''lo''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''ku''.&nbsp;<br>'''''lo'''''&nbsp;– generic begin convert selbri to sumti word. Extracts x1 of selbri to use as sumti.&nbsp;<br>'''''ku'''''&nbsp;– end convert selbri to sumti process.

|-
|You simply place a selbri between these two words, and it takes anything that can fill the x1 of that selbri and turns it into a sumti.&nbsp;<br>So for instance, the things that can fill zdani<nowiki>’</nowiki>s x1 are only things which are homes of somebody. So&nbsp;''lo zdani ku''&nbsp;means "a home or some homes for somebody." Similarly, if I say that something is pelxu, it means it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s yellow. So&nbsp;''lo pelxu ku''&nbsp;refers to something yellow.

|-
|Now you have the necessary grammar to be able to say "I am friends with an American." How?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi pendo lo merko ku''

|-
|There is a good reason why the&nbsp;''ku''&nbsp;is necessary. Try to translate "A German sells this to me"

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''lo dotco ku vecnu ti mi''&nbsp;If you leave out the ku, you do not get a bridi, but simply three sumti. Since lo…ku cannot convert bridi, the ti is forced outside the sumti, the lo-construct is forced to close and it simply becomes the three sumti of''lo dotco vecnu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki>'',&nbsp;''ti''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''mi''.

|-
|You always have to be careful with jufra like&nbsp;''lo zdani ku pelxu''. If the&nbsp;''ku''&nbsp;is left out the conversion process does not end, and it simply becomes one sumti, made from the tanru&nbsp;''zdani pelxu''&nbsp;and then converted with&nbsp;''lo''.

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons – lesson four (attitudinals)'''

|-
|Another concept which can be unfamiliar to English speakers is that of attitudinals. Attitudinals are words that express emotions directly. The idea of attitudinals originated in the feminist constructed language Ladan, supposedly to enable true female emotions. The idea was that female emotional expression was hindered by male dominated language, and if only they were able to be expressed more freely, this would empower women through liberation of the language.&nbsp;<br>In Lojban, there is no such agenda, and attitudinals most probably have been designed into the language because they turned out to be incredibly awesome and useful. They all have a so-called free grammar, which means that they can appear almost anywhere within bridi without disrupting the bridi<nowiki>’</nowiki>s grammar or any grammatical constructs.&nbsp;<br>In Lojban grammar, an attitudinal applies to the previous word. If that previous word is a word which begins a construct (like&nbsp;''.i''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''lo''), it applies to the entire construct. Likewise, if the attitudinal follows a word which ends a construct like&nbsp;''ku'', it applies to the ended construct.

|-
|Let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s have two attitudinals to make some examples:&nbsp;<br>'''''.ui''''': attitudinal: simple pure emotion: happiness - unhappiness&nbsp;<br>'''''za<nowiki>’</nowiki>a''''': attitudinal: evidential: I directly observe

|-
|Note that in the definition of&nbsp;''.ui'', there are listed two emotions, happiness and unhappiness. This means that&nbsp;''.ui''&nbsp;is defined as happiness, while its "negation", means unhappiness. "Negation" might be the wrong word here. Technically, the other definition of&nbsp;''.ui''&nbsp;is another construct,&nbsp;''.ui nai''. Most of the time, the second definition of attitudinals - the ones suffixed with&nbsp;''nai''&nbsp;- really is the negation of the bare attitudinal. Other times, not so much.&nbsp;<br>'''''nai'''''&nbsp;misc. negation - attached to attitudinals, it changes the meaning into the attitudinal<nowiki>’</nowiki>s "negation"

|-
|And some more selbri, just for the heck of it:&nbsp;<br>'''''citka'''''&nbsp;– x1 eats x2&nbsp;<br>'''''plise'''''&nbsp;– x1 is an apple of strain/type x2

|-
|The sentence&nbsp;''do citka lo plise ku .ui'', means "You eat an apple, yay!" (especially expressing that it is the&nbsp;'''apple'''&nbsp;that the speaker is happy about, not the eating, or the fact that it was you.) In the sentence&nbsp;''do za<nowiki>’</nowiki>a citka lo plise ku'', the speaker directly observes that it is indeed the&nbsp;'''"you"''', who eats an apple as opposed to someone else.

|-
|If an attitudinal is placed at the beginning of the bridi, it is understood to apply to an explicit or implicit&nbsp;''.i'', thus applying to the entire bridi:&nbsp;<br>''.ui za<nowiki>’</nowiki>a do dunda lo plise ku mi''&nbsp;– "Yay, I observe that you give an/some apple to me!"

|-
|''mi vecnu .ui nai lo zdani ku''&nbsp;"I sell (which sucks!) a home".

|-
|Try it out with a few examples. First, though, here are some more attitudinals:&nbsp;<br>'''''.u<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;attitudinal: simple pure emotion: guilt - remorselessness - innocence.&nbsp;<br>'''''.oi'''''&nbsp;attitudinal: complex pure emotion: complaint - pleasure.&nbsp;<br>'''''.iu'''''&nbsp;attitudinal: miscellaneous pure emotion: love - hate.

|-
|Look at that, a word with three emotions in the definition! The middle one is accessed by suffixinng with&nbsp;''cu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''. It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s considered the midpoint of the emotion.&nbsp;<br>'''''cu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;attitudinal midpoint scalar: attach to attitudinal to change the meaning to the "midpoint" of the emotion.

|-
|Try saying "I give something to a German, who I love"

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi dunda fi lo dotco ku .iu''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;instead of&nbsp;''fi''

|-
|Now "Aah, I eat a yellow apple"&nbsp;<br>Answer:&nbsp;''.oi nai mi citka lo pelxu plise ku''

|-
|Let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s have another attitudinal of a different kind to illustrate something peculiar:&nbsp;<br>''.ei''&nbsp;Attitudinal: complex propositional emotion: obligation - freedom.

|-
|So, quite easy: "I have to give the apple away" is&nbsp;''mi dunda .ei lo plise ku'', right? It is, actually! When you think about it, that<nowiki>’</nowiki>s weird. Why is it that all the other attitudinals we have seen so far expresses the speaker<nowiki>’</nowiki>s feeling about the bridi, but this one actually changes what the bridi means? Surely, by saying "I have to give the apple away", we say nothing about whether the apple actually is being given away. If I had used&nbsp;''.ui'', however, I would actually have stated that I gave the apple away, and that I was happy about it. What<nowiki>’</nowiki>s that all about?

|-
|This issue, exactly how attitudinals change the conditions on which a bridi is true, is a subject of a minor debate. The official, "textbook" rule, which probably won<nowiki>’</nowiki>t be changed, is that there is a distinction between "pure emotions" and "propositional emotions". Only propostional emotions can change the truth conditions, while pure emotions cannot. In order to express a propositional emotional attitudinal without changing the truth value of the bridi, you can just separate it from the bridi with&nbsp;''.i''. There is also a word for explicitly conserving or changing the truth conditions of a bridi:

|-
|'''''da<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;attitudinal: discursive: supposing - in fact&nbsp;<br>Saying&nbsp;''da<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;in a bridi changes the truth conditions to hypothetical, which is the default using propositional attitudinals. Saying&nbsp;''da<nowiki>’</nowiki>i nai''&nbsp;changes the truth condition to the normal, which is default using pure attitudinals.

|-
|So, what<nowiki>’</nowiki>s two ways of saying "I give the apple away"? (and feel obligation about it)

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi dunda lo plise .i .ei''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''mi dunda da<nowiki>’</nowiki>i nai .ei lo plise''

|-
|The feeling of an attitudinal can be subscribed to someone else using&nbsp;''dai''. Usually in ordinary speech, the attitudinal is subscribed to the listener, but it doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t have to be so. Also, because the word is glossed "empathy" (feeling others emotions), some Lojbanists mistakenly think that the speaker must share the emotion being subscribed to others.&nbsp;<br>'''''dai'''''&nbsp;attitudinal modifyer: Empathy (subscribes attitudinal to someone else, unspecified)&nbsp;<br>Example:&nbsp;''u<nowiki>’</nowiki>i .oi dai citka ti''&nbsp;- "Ha ha, this was eaten! That must have hurt!"

|-
|What often used phrase could&nbsp;''.oi u<nowiki>’</nowiki>i dai''&nbsp;mean?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"Ouch, very funny."

|-
|And another one to test your knowledge: Try to translate "He was sorry he sold a home" (remembering, that tense is implied and need not be specified. Also, "he" could be obvious from context)

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''u<nowiki>’</nowiki>u dai vecnu lo zdani ku''

|-
|Lastly, the intensity of an attitudinal can be specified using certain words. These can be used after an attitudinal, or an attitudinal with&nbsp;''nai''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''cu<nowiki>’</nowiki>''''i''&nbsp;suffixed. It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s less clear what happens when you attach it to other words, like a selbri, but it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s mostly understood as intensifying or weakening the selbri in some unspecified way:

|}


{|border="2" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4" width="38%"
|Modifying word
|Intensity

|-
|cai
|Extreme

|-
|sai
|Strong

|-
|(none)
|Unspecified (medium)

|-
|ru<nowiki>’</nowiki>e
|Weak

|}


{|border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding = "0" width="100%"
|&nbsp;&nbsp;<br>What emotion is expressed using&nbsp;''.u<nowiki>’</nowiki>i nai sai''&nbsp;?&nbsp;<br>'''''.u<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''''': attitudinal: simple pure emotion: amusement - weariness

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;Strong weariness

|-
|And how would you express that you are mildly remorseless?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''.u<nowiki>’</nowiki>u cu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i ru<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''

|-
|'''Lojban lessons – lesson five (SE)'''

|-
|Before we venture into the territory of more complex constructs, you should learn another mechanism for reordering the sumti of a selbri. This, as we will show, is very useful for making description-like sumti (the kind of sumti with&nbsp;''lo'').&nbsp;<br>Consider the sentence "I eat a gift", which might be appropriate if that gift is an apple. To translate this, it would seem natural to look up a selbri meaning "gift" before continuing. However, if one looks carefully at the definition of&nbsp;''dunda'', x1 gives x2 to x3, one realizes that the x2 of&nbsp;''dunda''&nbsp;is something given – a gift.&nbsp;<br>So, to express that sentence, we can<nowiki>’</nowiki>t say&nbsp;''mi citka lo dunda ku'', because&nbsp;''lo dunda ku''&nbsp;would be the x1 of&nbsp;''dunda'', which is a donor of a gift. Cannibalism aside, we don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t want to say that. What we want is a way to extract the x2 of a selbri.&nbsp;<br>This is one example where it is useful to use the word&nbsp;''se''. What&nbsp;''se''&nbsp;does is to modify a selbri such that the x1 and x2 of that selbri trade places. The construct of&nbsp;''se''&nbsp;<nowiki>+</nowiki> selbri is on its own considered one selbri. Let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s try with an ordinary sentence:&nbsp;<br>'''''fanva'''''''''&nbsp;= "x1 translates x2 to language x3 from language x4 with result of translation x5"&nbsp;<br>''ti se fanva mi''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''mi fanva ti''&nbsp;<br>This is translated by me (= I translate this). Often, but not always, bridi with&nbsp;''se''-constructs are translated to sentences with the passive voice, since the x1 is often the object taking action.&nbsp;<br>''se''&nbsp;has its own family of words. All of them swap a different place with the x1.

|}


{|border="2" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4" width="20%"
|se
|swap x1 and x2

|-
|te
|swap x1 and x3

|-
|ve
|swap x1 and x4

|-
|xe
|swap x1 and x5

|}


{|border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding = "0" width="100%"
|Note that s, t, v, and x are consecutive consonants in the lojban alphabet.

|-
|So: Using this knowledge, what would&nbsp;''ti xe fanva ti''&nbsp;mean?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"This is a translation of this" (or&nbsp;''fanva ti fu ti'')

|-
|''se''&nbsp;and its family can of course be combined with&nbsp;''fa''&nbsp;and its family. The result can be very confusing indeed, if you wish to make it so:&nbsp;<br>'''''klama'''''&nbsp;= "x1 travels/goes to x2 from x3 via x4 using x5 as transportation device"&nbsp;<br>''fo lo zdani ku te klama fe do ti fa mi''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''mi te klama do ti lo zdani ku''&nbsp;and since&nbsp;''te''&nbsp;exchanges x1 and x3: =&nbsp;''ti klama do mi lo zdani ku''&nbsp;<br>"This travels to you from me via a home." Of course, no one would make such a sentence except to confuse people, or cruelly to test their understanding of Lojban grammar.&nbsp;<br>And thus, we have come to the point where we can say "I eat a gift.". Simply exchange the sumti places of&nbsp;''dunda''&nbsp;to get the gift to be x1, then extract this new x1 with&nbsp;''lo''...''ku''. So, how would you say it?&nbsp;<br>One (possible) answer:&nbsp;''mi citka lo se dunda ku''&nbsp;<br>This shows one of the many uses for&nbsp;''se''&nbsp;and its family.

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban lessons – lesson six (abstractions)'''

|-
|So far we have only expressed single sentences one at a time. To express more complex things, however, you often need subordinate sentences. Luckily, these are much easier in Lojban than what one would expect.&nbsp;<br>We can begin with an example to demonstrate this: "I am happy that you are my friend." Here, the main bridi is "I am happy that X.", and the sub-bridi is "You are my friend." Looking at the definition for "happy", which is&nbsp;''gleki'':&nbsp;<br>'''''gleki'''''&nbsp;"x1 is happy about x2 (event/state)"&nbsp;<br>One sees that the x2 needs to be an event or a state. This is natural, because one cannot be happy about an object in itself, only about some state the object is in. But alas! Only bridi can express a state or an event, and only sumti can fill the x2 of&nbsp;''gleki''!&nbsp;<br>As you might have guessed, there is a solution. The words&nbsp;''su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''...''kei''&nbsp;is a generic "convert bridi to selbri" function, and works just like&nbsp;''lo''…''ku''.&nbsp;<br>'''''su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;x1 is an abstraction of <nowiki>{</nowiki>bridi<nowiki>}</nowiki> of type x2&nbsp;<br>'''''kei'''''&nbsp;end abstraction

|-
|Example:&nbsp;<br>'''''melbi'''''&nbsp;x1 is beautiful to x2.&nbsp;<br>'''''dansu'''''&nbsp;x1 dances to accompaniment/music/rhythm x2.&nbsp;<br>''melbi su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u dansu kei''&nbsp;- "Beautiful dancing"/"Beautiful dance"

|-
|It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s usually hard to find good uses of a bridi as a selbri. However, since&nbsp;''su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u BRIDI kei''&nbsp;is a selbri, one can convert it to a sumti using&nbsp;''lo''...''ku''.&nbsp;<br>Now we have the equipment to express "I am happy that you are my friend". Try it out!&nbsp;<br>'''''pendo'''''&nbsp;"x1 is a friend of x2"

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi gleki lo su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u do pendo mi kei ku''

|-
|However,&nbsp;''su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''…''kei''&nbsp;does not see much use. People prefer to use the more specific words&nbsp;''nu''…''kei''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''…''kei''. They work the same way, but mean something different.&nbsp;''nu…kei''&nbsp;treats the bridi in between as an event or state, and&nbsp;''du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u…kei''&nbsp;treats it as an abstract bridi, for expressing things like ideas, thoughts or truths. All these words (except&nbsp;''kei'') are called abstractors. There are many of them, and only few are used much.&nbsp;''su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u…kei''&nbsp;is a general abstractor, and will work in all cases.

|-
|Use&nbsp;''nu''&nbsp;to say "I<nowiki>’</nowiki>m happy about talking to you."&nbsp;<br>'''''tavla'''''&nbsp;x1 talks to x2 about subject x3 in language x4.

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi gleki lo nu tavla do kei ku''&nbsp;(notice both the English and the Lojban is vague as to who is doing the talking).

|-
|Other important abstractors include:&nbsp;''ka...kei''&nbsp;(property/aspect abstraction),&nbsp;''si<nowiki>’</nowiki>o...kei''&nbsp;(concept/idea abstraction),&nbsp;''ni...kei''(quantity abstraction) among others. The meanings of these is a complicated matter, and will be discussed much later, in lesson twenty-nine. For now, you<nowiki>’</nowiki>ll have to do without them.

|-
|It is important to notice that some abstractors have several sumti places. As an example,&nbsp;''du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;can be mentioned.&nbsp;''du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;is defined:&nbsp;<br>''du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;= "abstractor. x1 is the predicate/bridi of <nowiki>{</nowiki>bridi<nowiki>}</nowiki> expressed in sentence x2".&nbsp;<br>The other sumti places besides x1 is rarely used, but&nbsp;''lo se du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>bridi<nowiki>}</nowiki> kei ku''&nbsp;is sometimes used as a sumti for indirect quotation: "I said that I was given a dog" can be written&nbsp;''mi cusku lo se du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u mi te dunda lo gerku ku kei ku'', if you will pardon the weird example.&nbsp;<br>'''''cusku'''''&nbsp;x1 expresses x2 to x3 through medium x4&nbsp;<br>'''''gerku'''''&nbsp;x1 is a dog of race x2

|-
|'''Lojban lessons – lesson seven (NOI)'''

|-
|While we<nowiki>’</nowiki>re at it, there<nowiki>’</nowiki>s another type of subordinate bridi. These are called relative clauses. They are sentences which add some description to a sumti. Indeed, the "which" in the previous sentence marked the beginning of a relative clause in English describing relative clauses. In Lojban, they come in two flavors, and it might be worth distinguishing the two kinds before learning how to express them.&nbsp;<br>The two kinds are called restrictive and non-restrictive (or incidential) relative clauses. An example would be good here:&nbsp;<br>"My brother, who is two meters tall, is a politician." This can be understood in two ways. I could have several brothers, in which case saying he is two meters tall will let you know which brother I am talking about. Or I might have only one brother, in which case I am simply giving you additional information.

|-
|In English as well as Lojban we distinguish between these two kinds – the first interpretation is restrictive (since it helps restrict the possible brothers I might be talking about), the second non-restrictive. When speaking English, context and tone of voice (or in written English, punctuation) helps us distinguish between these two, but not so in Lojban. Lojban uses the constructs&nbsp;''poi…ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''noi…ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;for restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses, respectively.&nbsp;<br>Let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s have a Lojbanic example, which can also explain our strange gift-eating behaviour in the example in lesson five:&nbsp;<br>'''''noi'''''&nbsp;begin non-restrictive relative clause (can only attach to sumti)&nbsp;<br>'''''poi'''''&nbsp;begin restrictive relative clause (can only attach to sumti)&nbsp;<br>'''''ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;end relative clause

|-
|''mi citka lo se dunda ku poi plise ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;= "I eat a gift such that (something is) an apple".&nbsp;<br>Here the&nbsp;''poi…ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;is placed just after&nbsp;''lo se dunda ku'', so it applies to the gift. To be strict, the relative clause does not specify what it is, which is an apple, but since the relative clause applies to the gift, we can safely assume that it means that the gift is an apple. After all, in the context of lesson five, this seems reasonable. If we want to be absolutely sure that it indeed was the gift that was an apple, we use the word&nbsp;''ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'', which is a&nbsp;''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;(a Lojban pronoun, more on them later) representing the sumti which the relative clause is attached to.&nbsp;<br>'''''ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i; refers to the sumti, to which the relative clause it attached.

|-
|''.ui mi citka lo se dunda ku poi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a plise ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;= "Yay, I eat a gift which is an apple".&nbsp;<br>To underline the difference between restrictive and non-restrictive relative clauses, here<nowiki>’</nowiki>s another example:

|-
|'''''lojbo'''''&nbsp;"x1 reflects Lojbanic culture/community is aspect x2; x1 is Lojbanic."

|-
|''mi noi lojbo ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o fanva fo lo lojbo ku''&nbsp;= "I, who am a Lojbanic, translate from some Lojbanic language." Here, there is not multiple things which&nbsp;''mi''&nbsp;could refer to, and the fact that I am lojbanic is merely additional information not needed to identify me. Therefore&nbsp;''noi…ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;is appropriate.&nbsp;<br>See if you can translate this: "I flirt with a man who is beautiful/handsome".&nbsp;<br>'''''nanmu'''''&nbsp;"x1 is a man"&nbsp;<br>'''''melbi'''''&nbsp;"x1 is beautiful to x2 in aspect (ka) x3 by standard x4"&nbsp;<br>'''''cinjikca'''''&nbsp;"x1 flirts/courts x2, exhibiting sexuality x3 by standard x4"

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi cinjikca lo nanmu ku poi <nowiki>{</nowiki>ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a<nowiki>}</nowiki> melbi ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''

|-
|On a more technical side note, it might be useful to know that&nbsp;''lo <nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki> ku''&nbsp;is often seen defined as&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e noi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a <nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki> ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''.

|-
|Besides, it is also possible to connect two or more relative clauses to the same sumti, by using the relative clause joiner <nowiki>{</nowiki>zi<nowiki>’</nowiki>e<nowiki>}</nowiki>. It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s syntax is "sumti <nowiki>+</nowiki> relative clause <nowiki>+</nowiki> zi<nowiki>’</nowiki>e <nowiki>+</nowiki> relative clause (<nowiki>+</nowiki> zi<nowiki>’</nowiki>e <nowiki>+</nowiki> relative clause (...))". Here is an example:

|-
|'''''penmi'''''&nbsp;"x1 meets/encounters x2 at/in location x3"&nbsp;<br>'''''dasni'''''&nbsp;"x1 wears/is robed/garbed in x2 as a garment of type x3"

|-
|''mi tavla lo nanmu ku poi do penmi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o zi<nowiki>’</nowiki>e noi dasni lo xunre ku ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;<br>= "I talked to the man that you met and which (incidentally) was dressed in red."&nbsp;<br>(Literally: "... and which wears something red".)

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons – Lesson eight (terminator elision)'''

|-
|''.au da<nowiki>’</nowiki>i mi djica lo nu le merko poi tunba mi&nbsp;'''vau ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o ku'''&nbsp;jimpe lo du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u mi na nelci lo nu vo<nowiki>’</nowiki>a darxi mi&nbsp;'''vau kei ku vau kei ku vau kei ku vau'''''&nbsp;<br>- "I wish the American, who is my sibling, would understand that I don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t like that he hits me."&nbsp;<br>Regardless of whether the above sentence is being understood, (it shouldn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t, as it contains words we have not covered in these lessons yet) one thing stands out: As more complex Lojban structures are learned, more and more of the sentences get filled with&nbsp;''ku'',&nbsp;''kei'',&nbsp;''ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;and other of those words which by themselves carry no meaning.

|-
|The function of all these words is to signal the end of a certain grammatical construct, like for instance "convert selbri to sumti" in the case of&nbsp;''ku''. The English word for this kind of word is "terminator", the Lojban word is&nbsp;''fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''. They are written in bold in the example above.&nbsp;<br>Note: The&nbsp;''vau''&nbsp;in the above example are the fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o for "end bridi". There is a good reason you have not yet seen it, stay tuned.&nbsp;<br>'''''vau'''''&nbsp;fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o: Terminates bridi.

|-
|In most spoken and written Lojban, most fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o are skipped (elided). This greatly saves syllables in speech and space in writing, however, one must always be careful when eliding fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o. In the simple example&nbsp;''lo merko ku klama'', removing the fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o&nbsp;''ku''&nbsp;would yield&nbsp;''lo merko klama'', which is a single sumti made from the tanru&nbsp;''merko klama''. Thus, it means "an American traveler" instead of "an American travels". fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o elision can lead to very wrong results if done incorrectly, which is why you haven<nowiki>’</nowiki>t learned about it until now.

|-
|The rule for when fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o can be elided is very simple, at least in theory: "You can elide a fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o,&nbsp;'''if and only if'''&nbsp;doing so does not change the grammatical constructs in the sentence."&nbsp;<br>Most fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o can be safely elided at the end of the bridi. Exceptions are the obvious ones like "end quote"-fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o and "end bridi grouping"-fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o. This is why&nbsp;''vau''&nbsp;is almost never used – simply beginning a new bridi with&nbsp;''.i''&nbsp;will almost always terminate the preceding bridi anyway. It has one frequent use, however. Since attitudinals always apply to the preceding word, applying it to a fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o applies it to the entire construct which is terminated. Using&nbsp;''vau'', one can then use attitudinals afterthought and apply them to the entire bridi:&nbsp;<br>''za<nowiki>’</nowiki>a do dunda lo zdani <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> lo prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki>... vau i<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;- "I see that you give a home to a person... I approve!"&nbsp;<br>'''''prenu'''''&nbsp;x1 is a person; x1 has a personality.

|-
|Knowing the basic rules for fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o elision, we can thus return to the original sentence and begin removing fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o:

|-
|''.au da<nowiki>’</nowiki>i mi djica lo nu le merko poi tunba mi&nbsp;'''vau ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o ku'''&nbsp;jimpe lo du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u mi na nelci lo nu vo<nowiki>’</nowiki>a darxi mi&nbsp;'''vau kei ku vau kei ku vau kei ku vau'''''

|-
|We can see that the first&nbsp;''vau''&nbsp;is grammatically unnecessary, because the next non-fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o-word is&nbsp;''jimpe'', which is a selbri. Since there can only be one selbri per bridi,&nbsp;''vau''&nbsp;is not needed. Since&nbsp;''jimpe''&nbsp;as a selbri cannot be in the relative clause either (only one bridi in a clause, only one selbri in each bridi), we can elide&nbsp;''ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''. Likewise,&nbsp;''jimpe''&nbsp;cannot be a second selbri inside the construct&nbsp;''le merko poi<nowiki>{</nowiki>...<nowiki>}</nowiki>'', so the&nbsp;''ku''&nbsp;is not needed either. Furthermore, all the fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o at the very end of the sentence can be elided too, since beginning a new bridi will terminate all of these constructs anyway.&nbsp;<br>We then end up with:&nbsp;<br>''.au da<nowiki>’</nowiki>i mi djica lo nu le merko poi tunba mi jimpe lo du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u mi na nelci lo nu vo<nowiki>’</nowiki>a darxi mi''&nbsp;– with no fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o at all!

|-
|When eliding fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o, it is a good idea to be acquainted with&nbsp;''cu''.&nbsp;''cu''&nbsp;is one of those words which can make your (Lojbanic) life a lot easier. What it does is to separate any previous sumti from the selbri. One could say that it defines the next word to be a selbri, and terminates exactly as much as it needs to in order to do that.&nbsp;<br>'''''cu'''''&nbsp;elidable marker: separates selbri from preceding sumti, allows preceding fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o elision.

|-
|'''''prami'''''&nbsp;= "x1 loves x2"

|-
|''lo su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u do cusku lo se du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u do prami mi&nbsp;'''vau kei ku vau kei ku'''&nbsp;se djica mi''&nbsp;=&nbsp;<br>''lo su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u do cusku lo se du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u do prami mi&nbsp;'''cu'''&nbsp;se djica mi''&nbsp;<br>"That you say that you love me is desired by be" or "I wish you said you loved me"&nbsp;<br>note:&nbsp;''cu''&nbsp;is not a fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o, because it is not tied to one specific construct. But it can be used to elide other fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o.

|-
|One of the greatest strengths of&nbsp;''cu''&nbsp;is that it quickly becomes easy to intuitively understand. By itself it means nothing, but it reveals the structure of Lojban expressions by identifying the core selbri. In the original example with the violent American brother, using&nbsp;''cu''&nbsp;before&nbsp;''jimpe''&nbsp;does not change the meaning of the sentence in any way, but might make it easier to read.

|-
|In the following couple of lessons,&nbsp;''cu''&nbsp;will be used when necessary, and all fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o elided if possible. The elided fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o will be encased in curly brackets, as shown below. Try to translate it!&nbsp;<br>'''''vajni'''''&nbsp;"x1 is important to x2 for reason x3"&nbsp;<br>'''''jimpe'''''&nbsp;"x1 understands that x2 (du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u-abstraction) is true about x3"&nbsp;<br>'''''a<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- Attitudinal: Simple propositional emotion: Hope - despair

|-
|''a<nowiki>’</nowiki>o do noi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a lojbo .i<nowiki>’</nowiki>e <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> cu jimpe lo du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u lo fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> cu vajni <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>kei<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;<br>What do I state?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"I hope that you, a proud Lojbanist, understands that fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o are important"

|-
|Fun side note: Most people well-versed in fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o-elision do it so instinctively that they often must be reminded how important understanding fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o are to the understanding of Lojban. Therefore, each Tuesday have been designated "Terminator Day" or&nbsp;''fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o djedi''&nbsp;on the Lojban IRC chatroom. During Terminator Day, many people try (and often fail) to remember writing out all fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o with some very verbose conversations as a result.

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson nine (sumtcita)'''

|-
|So far we have been doing pretty well with the selbri we have had at hand. However, there is a finite amount of defined selbri out there, and in many cases the sumti places are not useful for what we had in mind. What if, say, i want to say that I am translating using a computer? There is no place in the structure of&nbsp;''fanva''&nbsp;to specify what tool I translate with, since, most of the time, that is not necessary. Not to worry, this lesson is on how to add additional sumti places to the selbri.&nbsp;<br><br>The most basic way to add sumti places are with&nbsp;''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o SELBRI fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;(yes, another example of a fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o,&nbsp;''fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''. It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s almost never necessary, so this might be the last time you ever see it.)&nbsp;<br>In between these two words goes a selbri, and like&nbsp;''lo SELBRI ku'',&nbsp;''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o SELBRI fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;extracts the x1 of the selbri put into it. However, with&nbsp;''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o SELBRI fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'', the selbri place is converted, not to a sumti, but to a&nbsp;''sumtcita'', meaning "sumti-label", with the place structure of the x1 of the selbri it converted. This&nbsp;''sumtcita''&nbsp;then absorbs the next sumti. One could say that using a&nbsp;''sumtcita'', you import a sumti place from another selbri, and add it to the bridi being said.&nbsp;<br>Note: Sometimes, especially in older texts, the term "tag" or "modal" is used for&nbsp;''sumtcita''. Ignore those puny English expressions. We teach proper Lojban here.

|-
|While it is hard to grasp the process from reading about it, an example can perhaps show its actual simplicity:&nbsp;<br>'''''skami'''''&nbsp;"x1 is a computer for purpose x2"&nbsp;<br>'''''pilno'''''&nbsp;"x1 uses x2 as a tool for doing x3"

|-
|''mi fanva ti fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o se pilno <nowiki>{</nowiki>fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u<nowiki>}</nowiki> lo skami <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;- "I translate this with a computer" The x2 of&nbsp;''pilno'', which is the x1 of&nbsp;''se pilno''&nbsp;is a place structure for a tool being used by someone. This place structure is captured by&nbsp;''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o SELBRI fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'', added to the main selbri, and then filled by&nbsp;''lo skami''. The idea of&nbsp;''sumtcita''&nbsp;is sometimes expressed in English using the following translation:&nbsp;<br>"I translate this with-tool: A computer"

|-
|A&nbsp;''sumtcita''&nbsp;can only absorb one sumti, which is always the following one. Alternatively, one can use the&nbsp;''sumtcita''&nbsp;construct by itself without sumti. In this case you need to put it either before the selbri or terminate it with&nbsp;''ku''. In such case one can think as if the sumtcita has the word&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;as the sumti.

|-
|'''''zukte'''''&nbsp;"x1 is a volitional entity carrying out action x2 for purpose x3"&nbsp;<br>'''''zarci'''''&nbsp;"x1 is a market/store/exchange/shop(s) selling/trading (for) x2, operated by/with participants x3"

|-
|''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o zukte <nowiki>{</nowiki>fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u<nowiki>}</nowiki> ku lo prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> cu klama lo zarci <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;- "By their own volition, a person is going to the store"

|-
|Note that there is&nbsp;''ku''&nbsp;in&nbsp;''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o zukte <nowiki>{</nowiki>fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u<nowiki>}</nowiki> ku''. Without it the sumtcita would have absorbed&nbsp;''lo prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;and we don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t want that.

|-
|We can say the same in other words:

|-
|''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o zukte <nowiki>{</nowiki>fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u<nowiki>}</nowiki> zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e lo prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> cu klama lo zarci <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;<br>''lo prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> cu fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o zukte <nowiki>{</nowiki>fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u<nowiki>}</nowiki> klama lo zarci <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''

|-
|retaining the meaning.

|-
|What does&nbsp;''mi jimpe fi la lojban fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o se tavla <nowiki>{</nowiki>fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u<nowiki>}</nowiki> mi''&nbsp;state?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"I understand something about Lojban, spoken to me"

|-
|Putting the&nbsp;''sumtcita''&nbsp;right in front of the selbri also makes it self-terminate, since sumtcita only can absorb sumti, and not selbri. This fact will be of importance in next lesson, as you will see.

|-
|Actually,&nbsp;''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;is not used very often despite its flexibility. What IS used very often, though, are BAI. BAI is a class of Lojban words, which in themselves act as&nbsp;''sumtcita''. An example of this is&nbsp;''zu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'', the BAI for&nbsp;''zukte''. Gramatically,&nbsp;''zu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;is the same as''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o zukte fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''. Thus, the above example could be reduced to:&nbsp;<br>''zu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e ku lo prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> cu klama lo zarci <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''. There exist something like 60 BAI, and a lot of these are very useful indeed. Furtermore, BAI can also be converted with&nbsp;''se''&nbsp;and friends, meaning that&nbsp;''se zu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;is equal to&nbsp;''fi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o se zukte fe<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'', which results in a great deal more BAI.

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson ten (PU, FAhA, ZI, VA, ZEhA, VEhA)'''

|-
|How unfamiliar to the English-speaker a language Lojban is when one can read through nine lessons of Lojban grammar without meeting a tense once. This is because, unlike many natural languages (most Indo-European ones, for instance), all tenses in Lojban are optional. Saying&nbsp;''mi citka lo cirla <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;can mean "I eat cheese" or "I ate the cheese" or "I always eat cheese" or "In a moment, i will have just finished eating cheese". Context resolves what is correct, and in most conversation, tenses are not needed at all. However, when it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s needed it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s needed, and it must be taught. Furthermore, Lojban tenses are unusual because they treat time and space fundamentally the same - saying that I worked a long time ago is not grammatically different than saying I work far away to the north.&nbsp;<br>Like many other languages, the Lojban tense system is perhaps the most difficult part of the language. Unlike many other languages though, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s perfectly regular and makes sense. So fear not, for it will not involve sweating to learn how to modify the selbri or anything silly like that.

|-
|No, in the Lojban tense system, all tenses are sumtcita, which we have conveniently just made ourselves familiar with. Okay okay, technically, tenses are slightly different from other sumtcita, but this difference is almost insignificant, and won<nowiki>’</nowiki>t be explained until later. In most aspects they are like all other sumtcita; they are terminated by&nbsp;''ku'', making it explicit that PU is terminated by&nbsp;''ku''.&nbsp;<br>There are many different kinds of tense-sumtcita, so let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s start at the ones most familiar to English-speakers.&nbsp;<br>'''''pu'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: before <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ca'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: at the same time as <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ba'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: after <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|These are like the English concepts "before", "now" and "after". In actuality though, one could argue that two point-like events can never occur exactly simultaneously, rendering&nbsp;''ca''&nbsp;useless. But&nbsp;''ca''&nbsp;extends slightly into the past and the future, meaning just "about now". This is because human beings don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t perceive time in a perfectly logical way, and the Lojban tense system reflects that.

|-
|Side note: It was actually suggested making the Lojban tense system relativistic. That idea, however, was dropped, because it is counter-intuitive, and would mean that to learn Lojban, one would have to learn the theory of relativity first.

|-
|So, how would you say "I express this after I came here?" (pointing to a paper)

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''mi cusku ti ba lo nu mi klama ti <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>kei<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''

|-
|Usually when speaking, we do not need to specify which event in the past this action is relative to. In: "I gave a computer away", we can assume that the action happened relative to "now", and thus we can elide the sumti of the sumtcita, because it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s obvious:&nbsp;<br>''pu ku mi dunda lo skami <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;or&nbsp;<br>''mi dunda lo skami <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;or, more commonly&nbsp;<br>''mi pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> dunda lo skami <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''. The sumti which fills the sumtcita is an implied&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'', which is almost always understood as relative to the speaker<nowiki>’</nowiki>s time and place (this is especially important when speaking about left and right). If speaking about some events that happened some other time than the present, it is sometimes assumed that all tenses are relative to that event which is being spoken about. In order to clarify that all tenses are relative to the speaker<nowiki>’</nowiki>s current position, the word&nbsp;''nau''&nbsp;can be used at any time. Another word,&nbsp;''ki''&nbsp;marks a tense which is then considered the new standard. That will be taught way later.&nbsp;<br>'''''nau'''''&nbsp;updates temporal and spacial frame of reference to the speaker<nowiki>’</nowiki>s current here and now.

|-
|'''''gugde'''''&nbsp;= "x1 is the country of people x2 with land/territory x3"

|-
|Also note that&nbsp;''mi pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> klama lo merko gugde <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>'', "I went to America", does not imply that I<nowiki>’</nowiki>m not still traveling to USA, only that it was also true some time in the past, for instance five minutes ago.

|-
|As mentioned, spacial and temporal time tenses are very much alike. Contrast the previous three time tenses with these four spacial tenses:&nbsp;<br>'''''zu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: left of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ca<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: in front of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ri<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: right of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''bu<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: at the same place as <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> (spacial equivalent of&nbsp;''ca'')

|-
|'''''o<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''''': attitudinal: complex pure emotion: patience - tolerance - anger

|-
|What would&nbsp;''.o<nowiki>’</nowiki>onai ri<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> nu lo prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> cu darxi lo gerku pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>kei<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;mean? (notice the first elided ku!)&nbsp;<br>'''''darxi'''''&nbsp;x1 beats/hits x2 with instrument x3 at locus x4

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"<nowiki>{</nowiki>anger!<nowiki>}</nowiki> To the right (of something, probably me) and in the past (of some event), something is an event of a person beating a dog." or "A man hit a dog to my right!"

|-
|If there are several tense sumtcita in one bridi, the rule is that you read them from left to right, thinking it as a so called "imaginary journey", Where you begin at an implied point in time and space (default: the speaker<nowiki>’</nowiki>s now and here), and then follow the sumtcita one at a time from left to right.&nbsp;<br>Example&nbsp;<br>''mi pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ba <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> jimpe fi lo lojbo fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;= "At some time in the past, I will be about to know about fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>os."&nbsp;<br>''mi ba <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> jimpe fi lo lojbo fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;"At some point in the future, I will have understood about fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>os."&nbsp;<br>Since we do not specify the amount of time we move back or forth, the understanding could in both cases happen in the future or the past of the point of reference.

|-
|Also, if spacial and temporal tenses are mixed, the rule is to always put temporal before spacial. If this rule is violated, it can sometimes result in syntactical ambiguity, which Lojban does not tolerate.

|-
|Suppose we want to specify that the a man hit a dog just a minute ago. The words&nbsp;''zi'',&nbsp;''za''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''zu''&nbsp;specifies a short, unspecified (presumably medium) and long distance in time. Notice the vowel order&nbsp;''i'',&nbsp;''a''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''u''. This order appears again and again in Lojban, and might be worth to memorize. "Short" and "long" in are always context dependent, relative and subjective. Two hundred years is a short time for a species to evolve, but a long time to wait for the bus.&nbsp;<br>'''''zi'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: Ocurring the small distance of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> in time from point of reference&nbsp;<br>'''''za'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: Ocurring the unspecified(medium) distance of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> in time from point of reference&nbsp;<br>'''''zu'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: Ocurring the far distance of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> in time from the point of reference

|-
|Similarly, spacial distance is marked by&nbsp;''vi'',&nbsp;''va''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''vu''&nbsp;for short, unspecified (medium) and long distance in space.&nbsp;<br>'''''vi'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: Ocurring the small distance of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> in space from point of reference&nbsp;<br>'''''va'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: Ocurring the unspecified(medium) distance of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> in space from point of reference&nbsp;<br>'''''vu'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: Ocurring the far distance of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> in space from the point of reference&nbsp;<br>'''''gunka'''''&nbsp;"x1 works at x2 with objective x3"

|-
|Translate:&nbsp;''ba <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> za ku mi vu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> gunka <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"Some time in the future, I will work a place long away"&nbsp;<br>Note: People rarely use&nbsp;''zi'',&nbsp;''za''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''zu''&nbsp;without a&nbsp;''pu''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''ba''&nbsp;in front of it. This is because most people always need to specify past or future in their native language. When you think about it Lojbanically, most of the time the time-direction is obvious, and the&nbsp;''pu''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''ba''&nbsp;superfluous!

|-
|The order in which direction-sumtcita and distance-sumtcita are said makes a difference. Remember that the meanings of several tense words placed together are pictured by an imaginary journey reading from left to right. Thus&nbsp;''pu zu''&nbsp;is "a long time ago" while&nbsp;''zu pu''&nbsp;is "in the past of some point in time which is a long time toward the future or the past of now". In the first example,&nbsp;''pu''&nbsp;shows that we begin in the past,&nbsp;''zu''&nbsp;then that it is a long time backwards. In the second example,&nbsp;''zu''shows that we begin at some point far away in time from now,&nbsp;''pu''&nbsp;then, that we move backwards from that point. Thus&nbsp;''pu zu''&nbsp;is always in the past.&nbsp;''zu pu''&nbsp;could be in the future. The fact that these time tenses combine in this way is one of the differences between tense sumtcita and other sumtcita. The meanings of other sumtcita are not altered by the presence of additional sumtcita in a bridi.

|-
|As briefly implied earlier, all these constructs basically treat bridi as if they were point-like in time and space. In actuality, most events play out over a span of time and space. In the following few paragraphs, we will learn how to specify intervals of time and space.

|-
|'''''ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: spanning over the short time of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: spanning over the unspecified (medium) time of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: spanning over the long time of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|'''''ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: spanning over the short space of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: spanning over the unspecified (medium) space of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;sumtcita: spanning over the long space of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|Six words at a time, I know, but remembering the vowel sequence and the similarity of the initial letter z for temporal tenses and v for spacial tenses might help the memorizing.&nbsp;<br>'''''.oi'''''&nbsp;- attitudinal: pain - pleasure

|-
|Translate:&nbsp;''.oi dai do ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> klama lo dotco gugde <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"Ouch, you spend a long time traveling a long space to Germany"

|-
|Though most people are not familiar with spacial tenses, these new words can open up for some pretty sweet uses. One could, for instance, translate "That<nowiki>’</nowiki>s a big dog" as&nbsp;''ti ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> gerku <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''. Saying: "This thing dogs for a long space" makes you sound retarded in English, but well-spoken in Lojban!

|-
|''ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;and its brothers also combine with other tenses to form compound tenses. The rule for&nbsp;''ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;and the others are that any tenses preceding it marks an endpoint of the process (relative to the point of reference) and any tenses coming after it marks the other endpoint relative to the first. This should be demonstrated with a couple of examples:&nbsp;<br>''.o<nowiki>’</nowiki>ocu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i do citka pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ba <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> zu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;- "<nowiki>{</nowiki>tolerance<nowiki>}</nowiki> you eat beginning in the past and for a long time ending at some point far into the future of when you started" or "Hmpf, you ate for a long time". One can also contrast&nbsp;''do ca <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>i <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> klama <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;with&nbsp;''do pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>i <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ca <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> klama <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''. The first event of traveling has one endpoint in the present and extends a little towards the past, while the second event has one endpoint in the past and extends only to the present (that is, slighty into the past or future) of that endpoint.&nbsp;<br>'''''jmive'''''&nbsp;"x1 is alive by standard x2"

|-
|What does&nbsp;''.ui mi pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> zi <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> jmive <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;express?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"<nowiki>{</nowiki>happiness!<nowiki>}</nowiki> I live from a little into the past and a long way towards the future or past (obviously the future, in this case) of that event" or "I am young, and have most of my life ahead of me&nbsp;
[[Image:Lojban_Wave_Lessons_Continued_25.png|framed|none]]
"

|-
|Just to underline the similarity with spacial tenses, let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s have another example, this time with spacial tenses:&nbsp;<br>'''''.u<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;attitudinal: wonder - commonplace

|-
|''.u<nowiki>’</nowiki>e za<nowiki>’</nowiki>a <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> bu<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ca<nowiki>’</nowiki>u <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> zdani <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;- What does it mean?

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"<nowiki>{</nowiki>wonder<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>I observe!<nowiki>}</nowiki> Extending a long space from here to my front is a home." or "Wow, this home extending ahead is huge!"

|-
|Before we continue with this syntax-heavy tense system, i recommend spending at least ten minutes doing something which doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t occupy your brain in order to let the information sink in. Sing a song or eat a cookie very slowly - whatever, as long as you let your mind rest.

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson eleven (ZAhO)'''

|-
|Though we won<nowiki>’</nowiki>t go through all Lojban tense constructs for now, there is one other kind of tense that I think should be taught now. These are called "event contours", and represent a very different way of viewing tenses that we have seen so far. So let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s get to it:

|-
|Using the tenses we have learned so far, we can imagine an indefinite time line, and we then place events on that line relative to the "now". With event contours, however, we view each event as a process, which has certain stages: A time before it unfolds, a time when it begins, a time when it is in process, a time when it ends, and a time after it has ended. Event contours then tells us which part of the event<nowiki>’</nowiki>s process was happening during the time specified by the other tenses. We need a couple of tenses first:

|-
|'''''pu<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi has not yet happened during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ca<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is in process during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''ba<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: The process of bridi has ended during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|This needs to be demonstrated by some examples. What<nowiki>’</nowiki>s&nbsp;''.ui mi pu<nowiki>’</nowiki>o <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> se zdani <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;mean?

|-
|Answer: "Yay, I<nowiki>’</nowiki>ll begin to have a home".

|-
|But hey, you ask, why not just say&nbsp;''.ui mi ba <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> se zdani <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;and even save a syllable? Because, remember, saying that you will have a home in the future says nothing about whether you have a home now. Using&nbsp;''pu<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'', though, you say that you are now in the past of the process of you having a home, which means that you don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t have one now.&nbsp;<br>Note, by the way, that&nbsp;''mi ba <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> se zdani <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;is similar to&nbsp;''mi pu<nowiki>’</nowiki>o <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> se zdani <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>'', and likewise with&nbsp;''ba<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''pu''. Why do they seem reversed? Because event contours view the present as seen from the viewpoint of the process, whereas the other tenses view events seen from the present.

|-
|Often, event contours are more precise that other kind of tenses. Even more clarity is achieved by combining several tenses:&nbsp;''.a<nowiki>’</nowiki>o mi ba<nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> zi <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> ba<nowiki>’</nowiki>o <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> gunka <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;- "I hope I<nowiki>’</nowiki>ve soon finished working."

|-
|In Lojban, we also operate with an event<nowiki>’</nowiki>s "natural beginning" and its "natural end". The term "natural" is highly subjective in this sense, and the natural end refers to the point in the process where it should end. You can say about a late train, for instance, that its process of reaching you is now extending beyond its natural end. An undercooked, but served meal, similarly, is being eaten before that process<nowiki>’</nowiki> natural beginning. The event contours used in these examples are as follows:

|-
|'''''za<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is in process beyond its natural end during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''xa<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is immaturely in process during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|'''''cidja''''': "x1 is food, which is edible for x2"

|-
|Translate:&nbsp;''.oi do citka za<nowiki>’</nowiki>o lo nu do ba<nowiki>’</nowiki>o <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> u<nowiki>’</nowiki>e citka zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e noi cidja do <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>’</nowiki>o<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>kei<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki>''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"Oy, you keep eating when you have finished, incredibly, eating something edible!"

|-
|
[[Image:Lojban_Wave_Lessons_Continued_26.png|framed|none]]
&nbsp;<br>Image above: ZAhO tenses (event contours). All tenses above the line of the event signify stages covering an amount of time. All tenses below the event line signify stages which are point-like.

|-
|All of these tenses have been describing stages of a process which takes some time (as shown on the graph above; those tenses above the event like). But many of the event contours describes point like stages in the process, like its beginning.
