As is true of&nbsp;''ca''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''bu<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'', they actually extend slightly into the past and future of that point, and need not to be precise.

|-
|The two most important point-like event contours are:&nbsp;<br>'''''co<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is at its beginning during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''co<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is at its ending during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|Furthermore, there is a point where the process is naturally complete, but not necessarily has ended yet:&nbsp;<br>'''''mo<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is at its natural ending during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>Most of the time, though, processes actually end at their natural ending; this is what makes it natural. Trains are not usually late, and people usually retrain themselves to eat only edible food.

|-
|Since a process can be interrupted and resumed, these points have earned their own event contour also:&nbsp;<br>'''''de<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is pausing during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>&nbsp;<br>'''''di<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: event contour: Bridi is resuming during <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|In fact, since&nbsp;''jundi''&nbsp;means "x1 pays attention to x2",&nbsp;''de<nowiki>’</nowiki>a jundi''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''di<nowiki>’</nowiki>a jundi''&nbsp;are common Lojban ways of saying "BRB" and "back". One could of course also say the event contours by themselves and hope the point gets across.

|-
|Finally, one can treat an entire event, from the beginning to the end as one single point using&nbsp;''co<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'':&nbsp;<br>'''''penmi'''''&nbsp;"x1 meets x2 at location x3"&nbsp;<br>''mi pu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> zi <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> co<nowiki>’</nowiki>i <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> penmi lo dotco prenu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>vau<nowiki>}</nowiki>''&nbsp;- "A little while ago, I was at the point in time where i met a German person"

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson twelve (orders and questions)'''

|-
|Phew, those two long lessons with syntax heavy Lojban gives the brain something to ponder about. Especially because it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s so different from English. So let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s turn to something a little lighter: Orders and questions.&nbsp;<br><br>What the...&nbsp;'''sit up and focus!'''

|-
|Since the way to express orders in English is to leave out the subject of the clause, why did you assume that it was you I was speaking to, and not ordering myself, or expressing the obligation someone else has? Because the English language understands that orders, by their very nature, are always directed towards the listener - the "you", and so the subject is not necessary.&nbsp;<br>In Lojban, eliding the subject yields&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'', so that possibility is sadly not open to us. Instead, we use the word&nbsp;''ko'', which is the imperative form of&nbsp;''do''. Grammatically and bridi-wise, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s equivalent to&nbsp;''do'', but it adds a layer of semantics, since it turns every statement with&nbsp;''ko''&nbsp;in it into an order. "Do such that this sentence is true for you=''ko''!" For the same reason we don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t need the subject in English sentences, we don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t need order-words derived from any other sumti than&nbsp;''do''.

|-
|How could you order one to go far away for a long time (using&nbsp;''klama''&nbsp;as the only selbri?)

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;ko ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>u ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u klama&nbsp;<br>(''.i za<nowiki>’</nowiki>a dai a<nowiki>’</nowiki>o mi ca co<nowiki>’</nowiki>u ciska lo fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o .i ko jimpe vau .ui'') - look up ciska and work it out.

|-
|Questions in Lojban are very easy to learn, and they come in two kinds: Fill in the blank, and true/false questions. Let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s begin with the true-false question kind - that<nowiki>’</nowiki>s pretty overcomeable, since it only involves one word,&nbsp;''xu''.&nbsp;<br>''xu''&nbsp;works like an attitudinal in the sense that it can go anywhere, and it applies to the preceding word (or construct). It then transforms the sentence into a question, asking whether it is true or not. In order to affirm, you simply repeat the bridi:&nbsp;<br>''xu ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>u zdani do''&nbsp;''.i ve<nowiki>’</nowiki>u zdani mi'', or you just repeat the the selbri, which is the bridi with all the sumti and tenses elided:''zdani''.&nbsp;<br>There is an even easier way to affirm using brika<nowiki>’</nowiki>i, but those are a tale for another time. To answer "no" or "false", you simply answer with the bridi negated. That too, will be left for later, but we will return to question answering by then.

|-
|The other kind is fill in the blank. Here, you ask for the question word to be replaced for a construct, which makes the bridi correct. There are several of these words, depending on what you are asking about:&nbsp;<br>'''''ma'''''&nbsp;- sumti question&nbsp;<br>'''''mo'''''&nbsp;- selbri question&nbsp;<br>'''''xo'''''&nbsp;- number question&nbsp;<br>'''''cu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;- tense question

|-
|As well as many others. To ask about a sumti, you then just place the question word where you want your answer:&nbsp;''do dunda ma mi''&nbsp;- asks for the x2 to be filled with a correct sumti. "You give what to me?". The combination of&nbsp;''sumtcita''&nbsp;<nowiki>+</nowiki>&nbsp;''ma''is very useful indeed:&nbsp;<br>'''''mu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;- sumtcita: motivated by the abstraction of <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>

|-
|''.oi do darxi mi mu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i ma''&nbsp;- "Oy, why do you hit me?!"

|-
|Let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s try another one. This time, you translate:&nbsp;<br>''.ui dai do ca ze<nowiki>’</nowiki>u pu mo''

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;"You<nowiki>’</nowiki>re happy, what have you been doing all this long time until now?" Technically, it could also mean "what have you been?", but answering with&nbsp;''.ua nai li<nowiki>’</nowiki>a remna''&nbsp;(Uh, human, obviously) is just being incredibly annoying on purpose.

|-
|Since tone of voice or sentence structure does not reveal whether a sentence is a question or not, one better not miss the question word. Therefore, since people tend to focus more on words in the beginning or at the end of sentences, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s usually worth the while to re-order the sentence so that the question words are at those places. If that is not feasable,''pau''&nbsp;is an attitudinal marking that the sentence is a question. Contrary,&nbsp;''pau nai''&nbsp;explicitly marks any question as being rhetorical.

|-
|While we are on the topic of questions, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s also appropriate to mention the word&nbsp;''kau'', which is a marker for "indirect question". What<nowiki>’</nowiki>s an indirect question, then? Well, take a look at the sentence:&nbsp;''mi djuno lo du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u ma kau zdani do''&nbsp;- "I know what is your home."&nbsp;<br>'''''djuno'''''&nbsp;"x1 knows fact(s) x2 are true about x3 by epistemology x4"&nbsp;<br>One can think it as the answer to the question&nbsp;''ma zdani do''. More rarely, one can mark a non-question word with&nbsp;''kau'', in which case one still can imagine it as the answer to a question:&nbsp;''mi jimpe lo du<nowiki>’</nowiki>u dunda ti kau do''&nbsp;- "I know what you have been given, it is this."

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson thirteen (morphology and word classes)'''

|-
|Back to more heavy (and interesting) stuff.&nbsp;<br>If you haven<nowiki>’</nowiki>t already, I strongly suggest you find the Lojbanic recording called "Story Time with Uncle Robin", or listen to someone speak Lojban on Mumble, and then practice your pronunciation. Having an internal conversation in your head in Lojban is only good if it isn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t with all the wrong sounds, and learning pronunciation from written text is hard. Therefore, this lesson will not be on the Lojban sounds, however important they might be, but a short introduction to the Lojban morphology.

|-
|What is morphology? The word is derived from Greek meaning "the study of shapes", and in this context, we talk about how we make words from letters and sounds, as contrasted with syntax - how we make sentences with words. Lojban operates with different morphological word classes, which are all defined by their morphology. To make it all nice and systematic though, words with certain functions tend to be grouped by morphological classes, but exceptions may occur.

|}


{|border="2" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4" width="100%"

|Meaning
|Defined By
|Typical Function

|Acts as a selbri by default. Always has a place structure.

|5 letters of the form CVCCV or CCVCV

{|border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding = "0" width="100%"
|&nbsp;&nbsp;<br><br>'''''cmevla'''''&nbsp;are very easy to identify because they begin and end with a pause, signaled by a full stop in writing, and the last letter is a consonant. cmevla can<nowiki>’</nowiki>t have any other function besides acting as a name. On the other hand, names which are not selbri cannot appear in Lojban without them being cmevla, or encased by certain quote words. One can mark stress in the names by capitalizing the letters which are stressed. Examples of cmevla are:&nbsp;''.iohAN.''&nbsp;(Johan, h is capital apostrophe),&nbsp;''.mat.''&nbsp;(Matt) and&nbsp;''.lutciMIN.''&nbsp;(Lui-Chi Min). Names which do not end in consonants have to have one added:''.ivyn.''&nbsp;(Eve), or (probably better in this case) removed:&nbsp;''.iv.''

|-
|'''''brivla'''''&nbsp;are called "bridi-words" because they by default are selbri, and therefore almost all Lojban words with a place structure are brivla. This has also given them the English nickname "content-words". It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s nearly impossible to say anything useful without brivla, and almost all words for concepts outside lojban grammar (and even most of the words for things in the language) are captured by brivla. As shown in the table, brivla has three subcategories:&nbsp;<br>'''''gismu'''''&nbsp;are the root words of the language. Only about 1450 exists, and very few new ones are added. They cover the most basic concepts like "circle", "friend", "tree" and "dream". Examples include&nbsp;''zdani'',&nbsp;''pelxu''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''dunda''&nbsp;<br>'''''lujvo'''''&nbsp;are made by combining rafsi (see under rafsi), respresenting gismu. By combining rafsi, one narrows down the meaning of the word. lujvo are made by an elaborate algorithm, so making valid lujvo on the fly is near impossible, with few exceptions like&nbsp;''selpa<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'', from&nbsp;''se prami'', which can only have one definition. Instead, lujvo are made once, its place structure defined, and then that definition is made official by the dictionary. Examples include brivla (bridi-word),&nbsp;''cinjikca''(sexual-socializing = flirting) and&nbsp;''cakcinki''&nbsp;(shell-insect = beetle).&nbsp;<br>'''''fu<nowiki>’</nowiki>ivla'''''&nbsp;are made by making up words which fit the definition for brivla, but not for lujvo or gismu. They tend to cover concepts which it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s hard to cover by lujvo, for instance names of species, nations or very cultural specific concepts. Examples include&nbsp;''gugdrgogurio''&nbsp;(Korea)&nbsp;''cidjrpitsa''&nbsp;(pizza) or&nbsp;''angeli''&nbsp;(angel).

|-
|'''''cmavo'''''&nbsp;are small words with one or zero consonants. They tend to not signify anything in the exterior world, but to have only grammatical function. Exceptions occur, and it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s debatable how much attitudinals exists for their grammatical function. Another weird example are the words of the class GOhA, which act as brivla. It is valid to type several cmavo in a row as one word, but in these lessons, that won<nowiki>’</nowiki>t be done. By grouping certain cmavo in functional units, though, it is sometimes easier to read. Thus,&nbsp;''.uipuzuvukumi citka''&nbsp;is valid, and is parsed and understood as&nbsp;''.ui pu zu vu ku mi citka''. Like other Lojban words, one should (but need not always) place a full stop before any words beginning with a vowel.&nbsp;<br>cmavo of the form xVV, CV<nowiki>’</nowiki>VV or V<nowiki>’</nowiki>VV are experimental, and are words which are not in the formal grammar, but which have been added by Lojban users to respond to a certain need.

|-
|'''''rafsi'''''&nbsp;are not Lojban words, and can never appear alone. However, several (more than one) rafsi combine to form lujvo. These must still live up to the brivla-definition, for instance&nbsp;''lojban''&nbsp;is invalid because it ends in a consonant (which makes it a cmevla), and&nbsp;''ci<nowiki>’</nowiki>ekei''&nbsp;is invalid because it does not contain a consonant cluster, and is thus read as two cmavo written as one word. Often, a 3-4 letter string is both a cmavo and a rafsi, like&nbsp;''zu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'', which is both the BAI and the rafsi for&nbsp;''zukte''. Note that there is nowhere that both a cmavo and a rafsi would be grammatical, so these are not considered homophones. All gismu can double as rafsi, if they are prefixed with another rafsi. The first four letter of a gismu suffixed with an "y" can also act as a rafsi, if they are suffixed with another rafsi. The vowel "y" can only appear in lujvo or cmevla. Valid rafsi letter combinations are: CVV, CV<nowiki>’</nowiki>V, CCV, CVCCy- CCVCy-, -CVCCV and -CCVCV.

|-
|Using what you know now, you should be able to answer the test i thus present:&nbsp;<br>Categorize each of the following words as cmevla (C), gismu (g), lujvo (l),&nbsp;''fu<nowiki>’</nowiki>ivla''&nbsp;(f) or cmavo (c):&nbsp;<br>A ) jai G ) mumbl&nbsp;<br>B ) .irci H ) .i<nowiki>’</nowiki>i&nbsp;<br>C ) bostu I ) cu&nbsp;<br>D ) xelman J ) plajva&nbsp;<br>E ) po<nowiki>’</nowiki>e K ) danseke&nbsp;<br>F ) djisku L ) .ertsa

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;a-c, b-f, c-g, d-C, e-c, f-l, g-C, h-c, i-c, j-l, k-f, l-f. I left out the full stops before and after names so it wouldn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t be too easy.&nbsp;<br>Note: some of these words, like&nbsp;''bostu''&nbsp;do not exist in the dictionary, but this is irrelevant. The morphology still makes it a gismu, so it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s just an undefined gismu. Similarly with&nbsp;''.ertsa''

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson fourteen (the Lojban sumti 1: LE and LA)'''

|-
|If you have read and understood the content of all the lessons until now, you have amassed a large enough knowledge of Lojban so that it doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t matter in which order you learn the rest. As a result, the order of the next lessons will be a mixture of sorted by increasing difficulty and sorted by importance in ordinary Lojban conversation.&nbsp;<br><br>One of the biggest constrains on your speak now is your limited knowledge on how to make sumti. So far, you only know''ti''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''lo SELBRI'', which doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t take you far considering how important sumti are in Lojban. This lesson as well as the following two will be about the Lojban sumti. For now, we focus on the descriptive-like sumti, the ones made with articles like&nbsp;''lo''&nbsp;<br>Articles are in lojban called&nbsp;''gadri'', and all the ones discussed in this lesson are terminated by&nbsp;''ku'', except the combinations''la CMEVLA'',&nbsp;''lai CMEVLA''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''la<nowiki>’</nowiki>i CMEVLA''. We will begin by describing three simple kinds of descriptive sumti, and then immediately find that they are not so simple after all:&nbsp;<br>'''''lo'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Generic veridical "convert selbri to sumti". Result is vague with regard to individuality/mass-ness.&nbsp;<br>'''''le'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Generic descriptive "convert selbri to sumti". Result is vague with regard to individuality/mass-ness.&nbsp;<br>'''''la'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Naming article: Conventional, "convert selbri or cmevla to sumti". Treat result as individual(s).

|-
|You are already familiar with&nbsp;''lo''&nbsp;and what it does. But what does it mean, "veridical" and "vague with regard to individuality/mass-ness"? The latter about individuals and masses, I<nowiki>’</nowiki>ll come back to later. For now, "veridical" in this context means that in order for a thing to qualify begin labelled as&nbsp;''lo klama'', it has to actually&nbsp;''klama''. Thus, veridical gadri makes a claim which may be true or false - that the object(s) in question are actually the x1 of the selbri after&nbsp;''lo''.

|-
|This may be contrasted with&nbsp;''le'', which is descriptive, and thus not veridical. Saying&nbsp;''le gerku''&nbsp;says that you have one or more specific objects in mind, and you use the selbri&nbsp;''gerku''&nbsp;to describe it, so that the listener may identify those specific objects. This means that&nbsp;''le''&nbsp;haves two important differences from&nbsp;''lo'': Firstly, it cannot refer to objects in general, but always refers to specific objects. Secondly, while&nbsp;''lo gerku''&nbsp;definitely is one or more dogs,&nbsp;''le gerku'', because it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s not veridical, can be anything, as long as the speaker thinks the description will help identifying the correct objects. Perhaps the speaker is referring to a hyena, but are not familiar with them and think "dog" is a good enough approximation to be understood. This non-veridicality is perhaps over-emphasised in most many texts; The best way to describe a dog is usually to describe it as being a dog, and unless there is a good reason not to,&nbsp;''le gerku''&nbsp;is usually presumed to refer to something which is also&nbsp;''lo gerku''.&nbsp;<br>In translation,&nbsp;''lo gerku''&nbsp;is usually "a dog" or "some dogs", while&nbsp;''le gerku''&nbsp;is "the dog" or "the dogs". Even better for&nbsp;''le gerku''&nbsp;would be "the "dog(s)" "

|-
|Last of the three basic&nbsp;''gadri'', there is&nbsp;''la'', the naming&nbsp;''gadri'', which I have unconventionally called "conventional". What I mean by this is that it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s neither descriptive nor veridical, since it refers to a proper name. If I in English refer to a person called Innocent by her name, I neither describe her as being innocent, nor do I state that she is. I only state that by convention, that object is referred to by that selbri or cmevla. Note that&nbsp;''la''&nbsp;and the gadri derived from it can convert cmevla to sumti unlike any other&nbsp;''gadri''. Also: Be cautious: Other texts do not mention that names can be formed from ordinary selbri using the gadri&nbsp;''la''. But those heretics must burn; selbri names are as good as they get, and many a proud Lojbanist have them.&nbsp;<br>''la'', as well as&nbsp;''lai''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''la<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;are a bit eccentric, since they&nbsp;'''always'''&nbsp;marks the beginning of a name. Unlike the other gadri, anything that can be grammatically placed after&nbsp;''la''&nbsp;and its sisters are considered part of the name. For example,&nbsp;''le mi gerku''&nbsp;is "my dog", but&nbsp;''la mi gerku''&nbsp;is someone called "My Dog".

|-
|These three basic&nbsp;''gadri''&nbsp;can be expanded with three more, which corresponds to the previous:

|-
|'''''loi'''''&nbsp;- gadri: veridical "convert selbri to sumti". Treat result as mass(es).&nbsp;<br>'''''lei'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Descriptive "convert selbri to sumti". Treat result as a mass(es).&nbsp;<br>'''''lai'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Naming article: Conventional, "convert selbri or cmevla to sumti". Treat result as mass(es).

|-
|These are the same in all aspects except for one: They treat the sumti explicitly as masses. If there is only one object in question, an individual and a mass consisting of one object are equivalent. The difference between these two concepts lie in which selbri can be ascribed to a group of individuals versus a mass. A group of individuals can be said to fit a certain selbri if, and only if, all members of the group each fit the selbri. It is correct to describe a pack of&nbsp;''lo gerku'', considered individually, as being black, if for each of the dogs it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s true that they are black. A mass, on the other hand, fits only those selbri which its components fit as a whole, as a team, so to speak. However, all the members of a mass&nbsp;''loi gerku''&nbsp;must be dogs in order for&nbsp;''loi''&nbsp;to be applicable. The notion of "masses" are sophisticated, and requires some examples to demonstrate which properties it can have:&nbsp;<br>'''''sruri''''': "x1 flanks/encircles/encloses x2 in line/plane/directions x3"&nbsp;<br>''lei prenu cu sruri lo zdani''&nbsp;- "The people surrounded the home." is plausible, even though, yo moma jokes not considered, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s completely implausible that it could be true for any one of the members alone. An English analogy could be: "Humans defeated smallpox in the 20th century". Surely no human did so, but the mass of humans did, and that makes the sentence true in English, as well as in Lojban if "humans" are a mass. Just like the Lojban mass, the English mass "humans" can only refer to individuals each of which are human. Another example:&nbsp;<br>'''''mivysle''''': "x1 is a biological cell of organism x2"&nbsp;<br>'''''remna''''': "x1 is a human"&nbsp;<br>''loi mivysle cu remna''&nbsp;- "Some masses of cells are human". Again, none of the cells are human. Indeed, the cells have very few human traits, but the cells considered as a whole makes up a human.

|-
|A mass made with&nbsp;''lei'', such as&nbsp;''lei gerku'', refers to a mass formed by a group of specific individuals, each of which the speaker refers to as&nbsp;''le gerku''.&nbsp;<br>Mass names as describes by&nbsp;''lai''&nbsp;are only appropriate if the group as a whole is named such, and not just if any of the members are. It can, however be used if the bridi is true for only a fraction of that group.

|-
|It is important to remember that&nbsp;''lo''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''le''&nbsp;can be used to describe both individuals and masses. Let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s say a pack of dogs, considered as a mass needs description. I might describe it as either&nbsp;''loi gerku''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''lo gerku''. If I use&nbsp;''lo'', this allows me to correctly state something which looks like a contradiction, but really isn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t:&nbsp;''lo gerku na gerku''&nbsp;- "Some dogs are not dogs". Since it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s being considered a mass of dogs, the many dogs consideres as a whole is not a dog, but rather a pack of dogs.&nbsp;<br>You might have noticed that there is no word which unambiguously converts selbri to individual(s). In order to be explicit about individualness, one needs&nbsp;''lo'',&nbsp;''le''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''la''&nbsp;with an outer quantifier. The subject of quantifiers will be considered later, in lesson twenty-two. What is the reason that&nbsp;''lo''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''le''&nbsp;vague, and not explicitly individual? It is because their vagueness enables them to be used in any context, without the speaker having to think about whether is behaves as a mass or a group of individuals.

|-
|Third in this series, there are three set-forming&nbsp;''gadri'':

|-
|'''''lo<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;- gadri: veridical "convert selbri to sumti". Treat result as a set.&nbsp;<br>'''''le<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Descriptive "convert selbri to sumti". Treat result as a set.&nbsp;<br>'''''la<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Naming article: Conventional, "convert selbri or cmevla to sumti". Treat result as a set.

|-
|Unlike groups of individuals or, sometimes, masses, sets does not take any of the properties from the objects from which the set is formed. A set is a purely mathematical or logical construct, and has properties like cardinality, membership and set inclusion. Again, note the difference between a set of things, and the things of which the set is formed:&nbsp;<br>'''''tirxu'''''&nbsp;"x1 is a tiger/leopard/jaguar of species/breed x2 with coat markings x3"&nbsp;<br>''lo<nowiki>’</nowiki>i tirxu cu cmalu''&nbsp;says nothing about whether big cats are small (which is, by the way, obviously false), but instead say that the set of big cats is small; that is - there are few of them.

|-
|Lastly, there are the (only two) generalizing&nbsp;''gadri'':&nbsp;<br>'''''lo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;- gadri: veridical "convert selbri to sumti". Sumti refers to the archetype of&nbsp;''lo <nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki>''.&nbsp;<br>'''''le<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;- gadri: Descriptive "convert selbri to sumti". Sumti refers to the described/perceived archetype of&nbsp;''le <nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki>''.&nbsp;<br>Of which there is no&nbsp;''la''-equivalent.

|-
|So, what is actually meant by the archetype? For&nbsp;''lo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e tirxu'', it is an ideal, imagined big cat, which has all the properties which best exemplifies big cats. It would be wrong to say that this includes having a striped fur, since a big systematic subgroup of the members of the set of big cats do not have striped fur, the leopards and the jaguars. Likewise, the typical human does not live in Asia even though a lot of humans do. However, if sufficiently many humans have a trait, for instance being able to speak, we can say:&nbsp;<br>'''''kakne''''': "x1 is capable of doing/being x2 under circumstance x3"&nbsp;<br>''lo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e remna cu kakne lo nu tavla''&nbsp;- "The typical human being can speak".

|-
|''le<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;then, is the ideal object as perceived or described by the speaker. This need not be factually correct, and is often translated as the "stereotype", even though the English phrase have some unpleasant negative connotations, which the Lojban does not. In fact, everyone has a stereotypical archetypichal image of any category. In other words,&nbsp;''lo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e remna''&nbsp;is the archetype which best exemplifies all&nbsp;''lo remna'', while the archetype&nbsp;''le<nowiki>’</nowiki>e remna''&nbsp;best exemplifies all&nbsp;''le remna''.

|-

However, the rules and definitions for gadri were changed in late 2004, and the current set of rules on this topic, nicked "xorlo" has replaced the old way. Now,&nbsp;''lo''&nbsp;is generic, and&nbsp;''xo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''is used as an elliptical digit (lesson nineteen).

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson fifteen (the Lojban sumti 2: KOhA3, KOhA5 and KOhA6)'''

|-
|See what happens if I try to translate the sentence: "Stereotypical people who can speak Lojban speak to each other about the languages they can speak":&nbsp;<br>'''''bangu'''''&nbsp;"x1 is a language used by x2 to express x3 (abstraction)"&nbsp;<br>''le<nowiki>’</nowiki>e prenu poi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a kakne lo nu tavla fo la .lojban. cu tavla le<nowiki>’</nowiki>e prenu poi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a kakne lo nu tavla fo la .lojban. lo bangu poi lo prenu poi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a tavla fo la .lojban. cu se bangu ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a''

|-
|What we see is that the Lojban version is much longer than the English. This is primarily because the first, ridiculously long sumti is being repeated two more times in the Lojban text, while the English can refer to it by "each other" and "they" - much more efficiently. Wouldn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t it be clever if Lojban somehow had mechanisms for doing the same?

|-
|It turns out it does, what a surprise! Lojban has a range of words called&nbsp;''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;meaning "sumti-representatives". In English, we refer to them as pro-sumti, because they are essentially the same as the English pronouns, but with sumti instead of nouns. In fact, you already know&nbsp;''ti'',&nbsp;''do''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''mi'', but there are many more, so let<nowiki>’</nowiki>s get learning. First, we want to put it into system. We can begin with the ones most familiar to English, and what you<nowiki>’</nowiki>ve already learned:

|-
|'''''ti'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: "immediate <nowiki>’</nowiki>it<nowiki>’</nowiki>: represents a sumti physically near the speaker"&nbsp;<br>'''''ta'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: "nearby <nowiki>’</nowiki>it<nowiki>’</nowiki>: represents a sumti some physical distance from the speaker OR close to the listener"&nbsp;<br>'''''tu'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: "distant <nowiki>’</nowiki>it<nowiki>’</nowiki>: represents a sumti physically far from the speaker and the listener."

|-
|You can again recognize the "i, a, u"-sequence which pops up over and over. Some things might take some clearing up, though. Firstly, these sumti can represent anything which can be said to occupy a physical space. Objects, certainly. Ideas, certainly not. Events are accepted, but only to the extent they are restricted to a specific place - the Jasmin Revolution cannot be pointed at, but some bar-fight or a kiss might. Secondly, note that the distance is relative to different things for the different words:&nbsp;''tu''&nbsp;only applies if it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s distant from both the speaker and the listener. In cases where the speaker and listener is far apart and the listener cannot see the speaker talking,&nbsp;''ta''&nbsp;refers to something close to the listener. Thirdly, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s all relative and context dependent. These three words are all problematic in written text, for instance, because the position of the speaker and listener is unknown to each other, and changes as time goes by. Furthermore, the author of a book cannot point to an object and express the pointing in the book.

|-
|Then there is a series called KOhA3, to which&nbsp;''mi''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''do''&nbsp;(and&nbsp;''ko'', but I won<nowiki>’</nowiki>t write that here) belongs:&nbsp;<br>'''''mi'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: The speaker(s).&nbsp;<br>'''''mi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: The mass of the speaker(s) and the listener(s) .&nbsp;<br>'''''mi<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: The mass of the speaker(s) and others.&nbsp;<br>'''''ma<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: The mass of the speaker(s), the listener(s) and others.&nbsp;<br>'''''do'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: The listener(s).&nbsp;<br>'''''do<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: The mass of the listener(s) and others.

|-
|These six sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i are more easily grasped in the below Venn diagram:

|-
|
[[Image:Lojban_Wave_Lessons_Continued_27.png|framed|none]]
&nbsp;<br>Venn diagram of KOhA3 (''ko''&nbsp;excluded).&nbsp;''le drata''&nbsp;is not a KOhA3, but means "the other(s)"

|-
|It is possible for several people to be "the speakers", if one statement is made on the behalf of all of them. Therefore, while "we" can be translated as either&nbsp;''mi'',&nbsp;''mi<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'',&nbsp;''mi<nowiki>’</nowiki>a''&nbsp;or&nbsp;''ma<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'', what one quite often means is really just&nbsp;''mi''. All of these six, if they refer to more than one individual, represent masses. Within bridi-logic, the bridi&nbsp;''mi gleki''&nbsp;said by speaker A is exactly equivalent to&nbsp;''do gleki''&nbsp;said by speaker B to speaker A, and are considered the same bridi. We will come back to this later, in the&nbsp;''brika<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;(pro-bridi) lesson.

|-
|All of these&nbsp;''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;are very content-specific, and cannot be used, for instance, to help us with the sentence which this lesson began with. The following series can in principle be used to refer to any sumti:&nbsp;<br>'''''ri'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: "Last sumti mentioned"&nbsp;<br>'''''ra'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: "A recent, but not the last sumti mentioned"&nbsp;<br>'''''ru'''''&nbsp;- sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i: "A sumti mentioned long ago"

|-
|These sumti will refer to any terminated sumti except most other&nbsp;''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''. The reason that most other&nbsp;''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''&nbsp;cannot be referred to by these sumti, is that they are so easy to just repeat by themselves. The exception to the rule are&nbsp;''ti'',&nbsp;''ta''&nbsp;and''tu'', because you could have changed what you point at, and thus cannot just repeat the word. They will only refer to terminated sumti, and thus cannot, for instance, be used to refer to an abstraction if the word in is that abstraction:&nbsp;''le pendo noi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a pendo mi cu djica lo nu ri se zdani''&nbsp;- here&nbsp;''ri''&nbsp;cannot refer to the abstration, since it is not terminated, nor to&nbsp;''mi''or&nbsp;''ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'', since they are sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i, so it refers to&nbsp;''le pendo''.&nbsp;<br>''ra''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''ru''&nbsp;are context-dependent in what they refer to, but they follow the rules mentioned above, and&nbsp;''ru''&nbsp;always refer to a more distant sumti than&nbsp;''ra'', which is always more distant than&nbsp;''ri''.

|-
|''ri''&nbsp;and it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s brothers are pretty well suited for dealing with the original sentence. Try saying it using two instances of''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i''!

|-
|Answer:&nbsp;''le<nowiki>’</nowiki>e prenu poi ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a kakne lo nu tavla fo la .lojban. cu tavla ru lo bangu poi ru cu se bangu ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a''.&nbsp;''ri''&nbsp;is not correct, because it refers to&nbsp;''la .lojban.''.&nbsp;''ra''&nbsp;could be used, but could be mistakenly be thought to refer to&nbsp;''lo nu tavla fo la .lojban.'', but''ru''&nbsp;is assumed to refer to the most distant sumti - the most outer one.

|-
|Lastly, there a sumtcita which represent utterances: So called utterance variables. They need not be restricted to one sentence (jufra), but can be several sentences, if the context allows it:&nbsp;<br>'''''da<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: Remote past sentence&nbsp;<br>'''''de<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: Recent sentence&nbsp;<br>'''''di<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: Previous sentence&nbsp;<br>'''''dei'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: This sentence&nbsp;<br>'''''di<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: Next sentence&nbsp;<br>'''''de<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: Near future sentence&nbsp;<br>'''''da<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: Remote future sentence&nbsp;<br>'''''do<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;Utterance variable: Elliptical utterance variable: "Some sentence"&nbsp;<br>These represents sentences as sumti, and refer only to the spoken words or the letters, not to the meaning behind them.

|-
|There are more Lojban&nbsp;''sumka<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'', but for now you probably need a break from them. The next lesson will be on derived sumti, sumti made from other sumti.

|-
|&nbsp;

|-
|'''Lojban Lessons - Lesson sixteen (the Lojban sumti 3: derived sumti)'''

|-
|You can probably see that the sumti&nbsp;''le bangu poi mi se bangu ke<nowiki>’</nowiki>a''&nbsp;is a less than elegant expression for "my language". This is because it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s really a work around. A language which I speak can be said to fill into the x1 of the bridi&nbsp;''bangu mi''. We can<nowiki>’</nowiki>t convert that to a sumti using a gadri:&nbsp;''le bangu <nowiki>{</nowiki>ku<nowiki>}</nowiki> mi''&nbsp;is two sumti, because&nbsp;''bangu mi''&nbsp;is a bridi, not a selbri. Neither can we convert it using&nbsp;''le su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u'', because the su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u gives the bridi a new x1, the abstraction, and the&nbsp;''le''&nbsp;then extracts that. That makes an abstraction sumti meaning something like "that something is my language".&nbsp;<br>Enter&nbsp;''be''.&nbsp;''be''&nbsp;is a word which binds constructs (sumti, sumtcita and others) to a selbri. Using it in ordinary selbri has no effect: in&nbsp;''mi nelci be do'', the&nbsp;''be''&nbsp;does nothing. However, when a sumti is bound to a selbri this way, you can use a gadri on the selbri without the sumti splitting off:&nbsp;''le bangu be mi''&nbsp;is a correct solution to the problem above. Likewise, you can attach a sumtcita:&nbsp;''le nu darxi kei be gau do'': "The event of hitting, which is caused by you". Note that the presence or absence of&nbsp;''kei''&nbsp;makes it parse differently: With the fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o present,&nbsp;''be''&nbsp;attaches to&nbsp;''nu'', without the fa<nowiki>’</nowiki>orma<nowiki>’</nowiki>o, it attaches to&nbsp;''darxi''. So it decides what is being emphasised: Is the hitting, or the event of hitting caused by you? In this specific case, though, that<nowiki>’</nowiki>s just about the same thing.

|-
|What if I want to attach several sumti to a selbri inside a gadri? "The giver of the apple to you" is&nbsp;''le dunda be lo plise be do'', right? Nope. The second&nbsp;''be''&nbsp;attaches to the apple, meaning&nbsp;''le plise be do''&nbsp;- "The apple of the strain of you", which makes no sense. In order to string several sumti to a selbri, the all the ones following the first must be bound with&nbsp;''bei''. The "binding" can be terminated with&nbsp;''be<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;- one instance of&nbsp;''be<nowiki>’</nowiki>o''&nbsp;for each selbri which has sumti bound by&nbsp;''be''.&nbsp;<br>To list them:&nbsp;<br>'''''be'''''&nbsp;binds sumti or sumtcita to selbri&nbsp;<br>'''''bei'''''&nbsp;binds a second, third, fourth (ect) sumti or sumtcita to a selbri&nbsp;<br>'''''be<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;ends binding to selbri

|-
|There is also ways to loosely associate a sumti with another.&nbsp;''pe''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''ne''&nbsp;for restrictive and non-restrictive association. Actually,&nbsp;''le bangu pe mi''&nbsp;is a better translation of "my language", since this phrase, like the English, is vague as to how the two are associated with each other.&nbsp;<br>''pe''&nbsp;and&nbsp;''ne''&nbsp;are used as loose association only, like saying "my chair" about a chair which you sit on. It<nowiki>’</nowiki>s not really yours, but has something do to with you. A more intimate connection can be established with&nbsp;''po'', which makes the association unique and binding to a person, as in "my car" for a car that you actually own. The last kind of associator is&nbsp;''po<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'', which makes a so-called "inalienable" bond between sumti, meaning that the bond is innate between the two sumti. Some examples could be "my mother", "my arm" or "my home country"; none of these "possesions" can be lost (even if you saw off your arm, it<nowiki>’</nowiki>s still&nbsp;'''your'''&nbsp;arm), and are therefore inalienable. Almost all of the times a&nbsp;''po<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;is appropriate, though, the x2 of the selbri contains the one to which the x1 is connected, so&nbsp;''be''&nbsp;is better.&nbsp;<br>'''''ne'''''&nbsp;non-restrictive relative phrase. "which is associated with..."&nbsp;<br>'''''pe'''''&nbsp;restrictive relative phrase. "which is associated with..."&nbsp;<br>'''''po'''''&nbsp;possesive relative phrase. "which is specific to..."&nbsp;<br>'''''po<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;inalienable relative phrase. "which belongs to..."

|-
|A very useful construct to know is&nbsp;''<nowiki>{</nowiki>gadri<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki>''. this is equivalent to&nbsp;''<nowiki>{</nowiki>gadri<nowiki>}</nowiki> <nowiki>{</nowiki>selbri<nowiki>}</nowiki> pe <nowiki>{</nowiki>sumti<nowiki>}</nowiki>''. For instance''le mi gerku''&nbsp;is equivalent to&nbsp;''le gerku pe mi''. One could have description sumti inside description sumti, saying&nbsp;''le le se cinjikca be mi ku gerku'', =&nbsp;''le gerku pe le se cinjikca be mi''&nbsp;="the dog of the man I<nowiki>’</nowiki>m flirting with", but that<nowiki>’</nowiki>s not very easy to read (or to understand when spoken), and is often being avoided.

|-
|One need also to learn&nbsp;''tu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'', since it will make a lot of sentences much easier. It takes a sumti and converts it to another sumti - an elliptical abstraction which has something to do with the first sumti. For example, I could say&nbsp;''mi djica lo nu mi citka lo plise'', or I could let it be up to context what abstraction about the apple I desire and just say&nbsp;''mi djica tu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a lo plise''. One always has to guess what abstraction the speaker means by&nbsp;''tu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a SUMTI'', so it should only be used when context makes it easy to guess. Another example:&nbsp;<br>'''''gasnu'''''&nbsp;"x1 does/brings about x2 (volition not implied)"&nbsp;<br>''za<nowiki>’</nowiki>a do gasnu tu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a lo skami''&nbsp;- "I see that you make the computer do something". Officially,&nbsp;''tu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a SUMTI''&nbsp;is equivalent to&nbsp;''le su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u SUMTI co<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''. Vague, but useful. There are situations where you cannot use&nbsp;''tu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'', even though it would seem suitable. These situations are when I don<nowiki>’</nowiki>t want the resulting sumti to be an abstraction, but a concrete sumti. In this case, one can use&nbsp;''zo<nowiki>’</nowiki>e pe''.&nbsp;<br>'''''tu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;convert sumti to vague abstraction involving the sumti. Equivalent to&nbsp;''le su<nowiki>’</nowiki>u SUMTI co<nowiki>’</nowiki>e kei ku''

|-
|Finally, one kind of sumti can be turned into another by the words of the class LAhE.&nbsp;<br>'''''lu<nowiki>’</nowiki>a'''''&nbsp;- Convert individual(s)/mass/sequence/set to individuals.&nbsp;<br>'''''lu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;- Convert individual(s)/mass/sequence/set to a set.&nbsp;<br>'''''lu<nowiki>’</nowiki>o'''''&nbsp;- Convert individual(s)/mass/sequence/set to mass.&nbsp;<br>'''''vu<nowiki>’</nowiki>i'''''&nbsp;- Convert individual(s)/mass/sequence/set to sequence; the order is not stated.&nbsp;<br>The use of these words is straight-forwardly: Placing them before a sumti of a certain type makes a new sumti of a new type. Notice, though, that as a fourth kind of sumti, a sequence has been introduced. This is not used very often (it doesn<nowiki>’</nowiki>t have its own gadri, for instance), but just included here for completion.&nbsp;<br>The last two members of LAhE do not convert between types of sumti, but allows you to speak of a a sumti by only mentioning something which references to it:&nbsp;<br>If one sumti A refers to a sumti B, for instance because sumti A is a title of a book, or a name, or a sentence (which always refer to something, at least a bridi), <nowiki>’’</nowiki>la<nowiki>’</nowiki>e SUMTI A''&nbsp;refers to sumti B. For instance, <nowiki>’’</nowiki>mi nelci la<nowiki>’</nowiki>e di<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;for "I like what you just said" (not&nbsp;''mi nelci di<nowiki>’</nowiki>u''&nbsp;which just means "I like your previous sentence") or <nowiki>’’</nowiki>la<nowiki>’</nowiki>e le cmalu noltru''&nbsp;for the book "The Little Prince", and not some little prince himself. The cmavo <nowiki>’’</nowiki>lu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e''&nbsp;does the exact reverse – <nowiki>’’</nowiki>lu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e SUMTI<nowiki>’’</nowiki> refers to an object which refers to the sumti.&nbsp;<br>'''''la<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;- "the thing referred to by" - extracts a sumti A from a sumti B which refers to A.&nbsp;<br>'''''lu<nowiki>’</nowiki>e'''''&nbsp;- "the thing referring to" - extracts a sumti B from a sumti A, when B refers to A.
